Description: This electronic text has been prepared from two manuscripts of an unpublished work. Ms. K is IFP transcript no. 333, which was copied from Ms. 5562 of the Government Manuscript Library in Chennai. Ms. Kh is deposited in the British Library in London; it is Sanskrit MSS 2541: IO ** ? 3 (or 8) 011. It is a transcript of a (likely South Indian) manuscript commissioned by H. T. Colebrooke in the first half of the 19th century. Both manuscripts are fairly accurate, though Ms. K is more so than Ms. Kh. There are a considerable number of manuscripts of this Kaula Tantra, which affiliates itself to the *Nityāṣoḍaśikārṇava*. These are virtually all found in South India. Notable features of this Tantra include extensive descriptions of *yonipūjā* and related rituals.

Salutations to Śrī Mahāgaṇapati. Salutations to Śambhu, the Great Liṅga, who is the root of bliss, the cause of joy for the world, and the eternal enjoyer. 1.1.1.
Śrī Devī questions Mahādeva Kāmeśvara, who is seated comfortably on the summit of Mount Meru and has the moon as his crest-ornament. 1.2.
The Śrī Devī said:
O God of gods, O Mahādeva, bestower of joy upon the world,
ocean of the nectar of compassion, stainless and untainted!
Salutations to You, the Independent One, whose form is the eternal support of the wheel of the world which lacks independence; [salutations] to You who grant whatever I ask. 1.4.
If you have a mind to show me favor, O Lord, please speak to me;
for you alone are proclaimed in all the scriptures as the dispeller of doubts.
O Śambhu, in every philosophical system and on every path, you alone are worshipped; there is no other person whatsoever.
O Maheśvara, since all your limbs are equal everywhere,
by what reason is the worship of your *liṅga* proclaimed as superior?
"You have not been worshipped on my head, nor at my feet, nor on my shoulders, nor even upon my chest; yet you, the Great Lord in the form of the Liṅga, have become pleased with me."
"O Lord, you ought to resolve this doubt of mine completely.
Kāmeśvara said:
"Listen, O goddess of beautiful hips; I shall tell you the reason for that."
He who, being the Supreme Brahman, is the partless Supreme Lord;
who dwells within the bodies of all deities and is the locus of the state of the individual soul (jīva).
That which is said to be of the nature of bliss— though existing everywhere, its own form is unmanifest to all— that state is called the *liṅga*.
That which is to be known as essence, Ānanda, is remembered as semen; indeed, from that very essence, having bound it, one becomes blissful. 1.12
That semen which, from the beginning of the Veda, attained the state of essence by means of valid cognition—that most exalted essence whose nature is bliss—[is this]. (1.13)
This sign is the sole path; therefore, it bears the form of bliss—it is the bulb of bliss, the seat of bliss, and the temple of bliss. 1.14
"Creator of the world, sustainer of the world, giver of life, embodiment of vital breath, and the most excellent of transmigratory existence—these are the glories of the Great Liṅga. (1.15)
The Liṅga is to be known as Paraśiva, and the place of the Bhaga is Maheśvarī;
the creation of the world arises from their union, and not otherwise, even in tens of millions of kalpas.
And the state of being a mere object of enjoyment for gods, humans, beasts, and even birds;
for kinnaras, siddhas, and even sādhyas. (1.17)
To all other living beings as well, in every respect,
I am the one whose nature is the Liṅga, bestowing the non-duality of existence and bliss.
For that very purpose, the activity of all is directed toward the Supreme Lord;
through the occasion of my worship, there is an abundance of joy for everyone. (1.19)
This state is the fulfillment of great bliss, the object of worship,
which has attained the form of a *liṅga* while being devoid of the light of the self.
4k) Therefore, this Maheśvara, who is of the form of a *liṅga* and named Ānanda,
was formerly entreated by me through the great *Ānandatantra*.
For that reason, this Tantra has come to wide circulation in the world;
indeed, all other Tantras are merely manifestations of the prosperity of this one. (1.22)
This tantra must be well-guarded, wherein bliss is proclaimed;
for all other scriptures, though manifest, are fruitless. 1.23
This secret Ānandatantra is said to be fruitful;
even while this tantra is being heard, there occurs a great flood of bliss. (1.24)
His mind dissolves into the Great Liṅga, which is the nature of bliss;
for they say that everything here is called a "liṅga" because of its capacity to cause dissolution. 1.25
If the mind is dissolved in the *liṅga*, its liberation (*kaivalya*) is certain;
I shall now explain this majesty of the *tantra* in brief. (1.26)
For those who maintain this tantra, read it, or even hear it; for those who practice it daily and discern its meanings as well— || 1.27 ||
For those who perform the ritual action as it has been prescribed therein,
my devotees shall experience the arising of non-dual bliss.
This tantra was previously proclaimed to the high-souled Keśava.
By him who, having manifested, remains within the purifying lineage of the Yadus. || 1.29 ||
This very same practice was performed by Kṛṣṇa among his sixteen thousand women;
it consists of the nature of existence (sat), the nature of consciousness (cit), and likewise the nature of bliss (ānanda).
All of that, as well as the engagement and withdrawal of all people in every respect, may be understood by the study of this treatise. (1.31)
The supreme reality is known through the study of this tantra, even for one who has not received the Kaulika initiation and by whom the Guru has not been worshipped. (1.32)
He who has no true devotion toward me, he by whom nothing has been composed for that purpose,
he who lacks the desire to know reality— for him you do not grant your grace.
This tantra, characterized by bliss, is indeed difficult for him to obtain;
having heard it even once therein, one is liberated from all sins.
When misfortune and distress arise, or when there is fear born of thieves, tigers, and the like—in all such cases within this transmigratory world, happiness shall emerge through this Tantra. (1.35)
One without offspring shall obtain sons, and [a woman] shall obtain daughters endowed with auspicious marks;
a poor man shall obtain great wealth, and one afflicted by disease shall obtain freedom from illness.
By the recitation of this tantra, one who is devoid of qualities becomes possessed of qualities;
herein lies the supreme reality, the most excellent within the Mantra-tantra.
Everything else is but the prattle of a drunkard, a mockery of the scriptures, or the ravings of a madman; it is remembered as nothing more than weeping in the wilderness. (1.38)
Sowing seed in barren soil is like [teaching] this tantra to one who is merely ignorant of the Self;
therefore, the hero who is devoted to the Guru [should teach it]. (1.39)
One who has ascertained the true meaning of the scriptures should grasp this for the sake of his own realization;
for that dull-witted person who [seeks it] through another scripture, this tantra is more worthy of veneration. (1.40)

6k) That person of deluded mind who, having seen this tantra, will remain indifferent toward it—him the awakened one should weigh against the state of those fallen into the calamities of the Vedas. || 1.41 ||
For seven births he shall be a fool and is born without offspring—
he dull-witted man who reviles this tantra characterized by bliss. (1.42)
He is born as a eunuch for the duration of a thousand births;
[he who does not worship] Ānandadeva, the Lord (Īśāna) of this great Tantra. 1.43
He who performs that sacrifice when it has arrived shall become an inhabitant of the Raurava hell;
therefore, this tantra, having been obtained, must be protected with great effort.
It should be worshipped with flowers and other offerings, and kept within one's own home;
it should be beheld with every effort and practiced with reverence. || 1.45 ||
Having practiced this Tantra of great success many times for one's own purposes, O beloved, this majesty of the Ānanda-tantra has been told to you.
"In this regard, I shall declare to you the reality of the sign of consciousness.
Thus ends the first [chapter] in the *Nityāṣoḍaśikārṇava* Tantra, which extends to thirty-two crores [of verses], within the *Bhagamālinī-saṃhitā* of the hundred-thousand-verse *Ānanda-tantra*.
Chapter One.
The second chapter.
Śrī Kāmeśvara said: O Mahādevī of virtuous vows, listen once more; I shall speak.
O Maheśvarī, this Liṅga is the abode of the goddess Ānandā.
Through that means, hear also the form of the sacred field (kṣetra) of the devotee of Śiva:
when, by the descent of his own power, he becomes awakened and possesses reflective awareness (vimarśa). (2.2)
A person should attain the realization that the Guru is of the very nature of Śiva;
then that teacher, through his vision of Śiva, [perceives] that disciple as a new self. (2.3)
For a devotee who is exceedingly devoted, it shall utterly burn away the fetter of the individual soul (paśupāśa);
for the high-souled Kaulika, however, it shall become something entirely different.
Compassion, apprehension, fear, shame, and disgust as the fifth;
family, caste, and character—these eight are proclaimed to be the snares (pāśas). (2.5)
If these bonds have been burnt away by the Guru, the remover of sin, then the entire body of that devotee is called a fertile field. (2.6)
Three initiations are proclaimed: the Śākta, the Māntrī, and the Śāmbhavī.
The Śākta [initiation] occurs through the unfolding of power (śakti), and the Māntrī through the instruction of mantras. (2.7)
The Śāmbhavī [initiation] is located in the middle of the head, within the red and white lotuses;
by these three initiations, a man is truly initiated. (2.8)

When beheld with the perfect glances of the Guru, which are thick with compassion, this [Self], whose true nature is the Linga of Awakening, arises through the exhaustion of latent impressions (vāsanā). (2.9)
Anger, greed, as well as delusion, lust, envy, and intoxication; that which is censured by women, censured by the world, as well as laziness and fickleness. (2.10)
Deluded vision, as well as pride, meditation upon others, violating another's wife, and the contemplation of malice toward others. (2.11)
Censuring others, harsh speech, quarreling, wicked conduct, an excessively cruel disposition, extreme wretchedness, and excessive greed. (2.12)
8k) Being afflicted by an incurable disease, extreme poverty, and so forth—such great defects arise from the very sight of the teacher. (2.13)
Through the greatness of the Guru and by the power of faith, the arts, sciences, passion, destiny, and time itself are consumed. (2.14)
Māyā is the limit of Maheśa; all obstructive powers (śaktis) consist of these very intense powers known as the eight coverings (kañcukas).

The Lord, whose form is accompanied by them, assumes the state of the individual soul (jīva). Having attained the state of the individual soul through them, he moves about like one who is transmigrating.
Bound by one pleasure after another, the individual soul wanders through the perils of discontent; carried here and there, it reflects upon itself by its own power. (2.17)

Having perceived Śiva as one's own essential nature, one is liberated spontaneously and swiftly; therefore, the state of being a limited individual (jīvatva) is suppressed for those who take refuge in Śiva-nature. Upon the destruction of the impurities (mala), the individual soul itself becomes the Great Lord (Maheśvara).
Just as a reflection does not appear in a tarnished mirror due to its lack of capacity. || 2/19 ||
In the same way, the soul (jīva), when clouded by impurity (mala), does not find the path of reality (tattvamārga).
Therefore, through the destruction of that impurity, the attainment of the state of Śiva occurs. (2.20)
The body of this pure devotee is called a fertile field;
yet, due to the power of beginningless ignorance, it may contain a great mass of impurity. (2.21)
In that state, this meditation is remembered as producing a dense darkness;
it burns intensely like ten million fires of cosmic destruction, blazing with radiant nooses. (2.22)
One should meditate upon one's own power, which has emerged from Brahman as if devouring the cosmic eggs on all sides, and which has been purified by the gaze of the Guru. (2.23)
As long as there is the burning of the noose and as long as the destruction of the foul qualities continues, so long should this meditation be practiced, which cuts away all impurities. (2.24)
By means of this yoga of meditation, when impurity has dissolved from the mandala,
one's own self shines forth spontaneously as a vessel of auspiciousness.
When the lamp-vessel that contains it is destroyed by the blow of a staff,
the lamp situated within shines forth by means of its luminosity. (2.26)
In the same way, when the chamber of impurities has been destroyed by the teacher in an instant,
the Self, which illuminates the universe, shines like the midday sun. (2.27)
Then this Self alone, residing within the pure body of the devotee,
becomes manifest externally through its manifold, radiant qualities.
For the embodied soul whose mass of impurities has been burnt away by the light of the Teacher, his qualities become manifest, through which Śiva is inferred. (2.29)
Upon seeing that devotee, he who was angry becomes gracious by force;
even the mind of those who have committed offenses trembles in an instant. (2.30)
His splendor increases, removing the pride of the god of love; even though his age has reached its full extent, he attains the bloom of youth. (2.31)
The accomplishment of his every resolve, the winning over of all people, unimpeded movement everywhere, and the health of his sense organs. (2.32)
The body of a devotee, which has attained the Supreme Self manifested through such qualities and serves as His dwelling place, is called a "sukṣetra" (an excellent field). 2/33.
Whatever objective realities exist within the fourteen worlds, they abide within the body of the devotee in an extremely subtle form. (2.34)
Aṭala is in the region of the hips, Vitala at the boundary of the thighs, Sutala situated at the boundary of the knees, and Talātala in the shanks. (2.35)
Rasātala should be at the ankles, and Pātāla at the toes;
that which is known as Mahāpātāla is said to be on the soles of the feet.
Furthermore, the world of Bhūr is in the Ādhāra, and likewise the world of Bhuvas is in the Svādhiṣṭhāna;
the world of Suvar is in the Maṇipūra, while the world of Mahar is in the Anāhata. (2.37)
The world of humans (janaloka) is at the edge of the throat; the world of asceticism (tapoloka) is situated in the region of purification;
and the world of truth (satyaloka) is in the aperture of Brahmā (brahmabila). Thus, there are fourteen worlds. (2/38)
Having entered the body of the devotee and remaining there in a subtle form, the *iḍā* channel becomes the Gaṅgā, and the *piṅgalā* likewise becomes the Yamunā. (2.39)
Sarasvatī is Suṣumnā, and Kāśī is the region between the eyebrows; indeed, all sacred fords (tīrthas) are situated within the locus of the Mātṛkās. (2.40)
Pauṣkara, the Naimiṣa forest, Kedāra, Harimedinī, the hermitage of Badarī, Uṣṇāmbu, Śītāmbu, and the Girikāvana; 2/41.
Dārukā, other forests, sacred fords (tīrthas), holy places (sthānakas), all fields (kṣetras), and various pīṭhas as well. || 2.42 ||
The divine seats named Kāpū, Ojā, and so forth, belonging to Śāṅkarī, are the stainless abodes of the Mother for the devotee. (2.43)
Thus, for me, the embodied devotee who has become all parts, there exists the fifteenth world, whose form consists of bliss. (2.44)
Transcending the world and stainless, he is untouched by sufferings;
he is ever endowed with the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra) and is eternally devoted to enjoyment. (2.45)
O Ānanda, the enjoyment of the devotee is established at the base of the Liṅga;
there, in the great world of bliss, he assumes the form of supreme nectar.
The great white ocean, which is the seed for the creation of the three worlds,
has its vast waves moving across and pervading the quarters of space.
The wind of consciousness abiding in its own place, which has deluded the world with touch, is exceedingly pure and white, the very form of bliss, and the bestower of happiness. (2/48)
In the midst of that, situated upon a jeweled boat is the pleasure-throne (ratisiṃhāsana), where resides the god Ānandabhairava, the bestower of bliss upon the world. (2.49)
The Ānandabhairava-yantra was likewise obtained and joined together;
thus Maheśvara, in the form of a Liṅga, attained the state of the nature of bliss (ānandarūpatā). || 2/50 ||
It exists in a subtle form, pervading all things even while remaining present;
therefore, the body of a devotee must never be reviled by those of dull intellect. (2.51)
He who reviles a shrine of Śiva by describing it as a mass of flesh and bone, a foul defect, or as excrement and urine, shall indeed go to the state of the foot of a dog. (2.52)
Therefore, my devotee should not despise his own body;
he should always protect himself, for the self is the refuge of all people. (2.53)
The field of accomplishment (siddhikṣetra) has the form of devotees, and otherwise the form of non-devotees;
here, the essential nature of those non-devotee forms is described.
It is soiled, fraught with great defects, crowded with manifold impurities, possessed of the delusions of many minds, and a sole abode of suffering. (2.55)

It is a consciousness that perceives pleasure in what is not pleasant, and it fails to recognize pleasure even when it is present; it is afflicted by loathing and corrupted by sleep, laziness, and the like. (2.56)
Swollen by the power of corrupt food, miserable, filled with foul impurities, devoid of self-knowledge, it is the very embodiment of hell visible before one's eyes. (2.57)
It was unattractive and inauspicious, hissed at by throngs of women; it was devoid of all aesthetic charm and defiled by many who were hostile to it. (2.58)
The body of one who is not a devotee is to be known as such; Ānandamaheśvara is not present here [in that body].
Therefore, Maheśvara resides at the base of the *liṅga* within the body of a devotee. (2.59)
The leader Ānanda has been proclaimed as the consort of the goddess Bhairavī;
thus ends the second chapter in the Ānandatantra. 2/2.
The Third Chapter. Now, O Goddess of the Gods, I shall explain how the entire path of the scriptures culminates precisely in the worship of Ānandanātha.
O Bhairavī, many systems of philosophy have been created by me, as well as an exceedingly great number of scriptures and their commentaries, O wise one. (3.2)
13k) However, all systems of philosophy and all treatises in every respect are beneficial to the path of the Veda alone, whether directly or indirectly. (3/3)
The treatise on the instruction of words, which discriminates between the correct and the incorrect, shall become known as Nirukta for the purpose of explaining the Veda. (3.4)
The *Chandoviditatantra* is the instruction on Vedic meters, while the *Śikṣā-śāstra* is the analysis of the phonemes situated within the Vedas. (3.5)

The compilation of the network of rituals prescribed in the Vedas is derived from the Kalpasūtras; the science of astrology (jyotiṣa) provides instruction on the solar transits and the new and full moon sacrifices, and so forth. (3/6)
Thus, accompanied by these six limbs, he is the initiator of Vedic rites;
indeed, there are also other external limbs of the Vedas.
Mīmāṃsā is the means of discerning the statements of those devoted to the Śruti; through Nyāya there is reflection on reasons, and through the Purāṇas comes the determination of reality. (3.8)
The Dharmaśāstra is the promoter of the right conduct of those who follow the Veda;
by these auxiliary limbs as well, the path of the Veda is refined. (3.9)
O Goddess, that very [Veda] becomes fourfold by the power of primordial nature (prakṛti);
through the divisions of Sāman, Ṛg, Yajus, and Atharvan, the arrangement of sacrifice is established. (3.10)
O Maheśvarī, the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma and other sacrifices— which are taught in the Vedas and which possess various states and distinctions— is heaven.
And heaven would consist of happiness, and happiness is characterized by bliss.
Heaven is said to be of two kinds: either a place or happiness itself. (3.12)
First, however, there is the Goddess; she is called the means for attaining happiness.
Heaven is the means for happiness, and the place is the means for that. (3.13)
This sequence is recorded as the order for the previously mentioned position regarding sacrificial acts:
"If heaven were merely happiness, there would indeed be no restriction of place here. (3.14)
In whatever state one experiences happiness, that is the fruit of performing sacrifices for heaven;
however, in the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa), the attainment of the fruits of sacrifices is what is being discussed.
When a sacrifice such as the Jyotiṣṭoma has been performed and completed, an *apūrva* (unseen potency) arises from it; that [potency] resides in the self. (3.16)

By that aforementioned means of valid cognition, namely presumptive testimony (arthāpatti), which resides solely within the self and perishes even at the end of one's experience, [the existence of the self is established]. (3.17)
Being suddenly drawn upward at the end of the body, one enjoys heaven;
at the end of the faults of the kutas, one is proclaimed as dwelling in heaven. (3.18)
Thirty-two crores of gods and sixty-six crores of goddesses dwell there constantly, thronging at the feet of those who drink nectar. (3.19)
Those who are proficient in pure bliss, eternally satisfied, and free from affliction—the sacrificer, having gone there, [is honored] by the hosts of deities residing there. (3.20)
He beholds his own imagined dwelling, beautiful, filled with pillars of jewels and strewn with nets of pearls. (3.21)
Equipped with articles of enjoyment, adorned with canopies and mirrors,
and fragrant with the fresh incense-sticks produced from black agallochum.
It was adorned with wish-fulfilling trees (*kalpavṛkṣa*) consisting of the most excellent substances that bestow enjoyments, and with jeweled jars filled with sweet honey. (3.23)
It was crowded here and there with fragrant articles, flower garlands, beds, and craftsmen, as well as groups of clever female attendants. (3.24)
Having gone to heaven as a divine being, he beholds a single beautiful-eyed woman, whose form causes even the fire of the world to become utterly intoxicated.

With glances that were bashful, smiling, imbued with emotion, and overflowing with passion—glances woven with subtle intentions and directed toward the corners of her eyes—she appeared exceedingly beautiful. (3.26)
Engaged with her in the playful movements of Taraloma, he gradually enjoys the pleasure of the contact between limb and limb, which is appropriate for that moment.
Due to the excellence of the place, the excellence of the body, and the excellence of the time,
that very same bliss of *liṅga* appears as if it were something different. (3/28)
Beholding the vast difference between the happiness of humans and that of the gods,
the sacrificer marvels at his own means of accomplishing ritual action.
The Goddess worships the Lord situated at the base of the *liṅga*, who is characterized by the arising of bliss,
with offerings of the flower of her womb.
Therefore, O Ānanda, the supreme fruit of all the sacrificial rites proclaimed in the entirety of the Vedas, when performed, is indeed the propitiation of the God. (3.31)
Therefore, the ultimate purport of the Veda itself—the most exalted and preeminent of all scriptures—is the sequence of worshiping the Great Liṅga. (3.32)
This fruit is declared to belong to other systems of philosophy as well;
however, the essence of Āyurveda is said to be *vājīkaraṇa* (aphrodisiac therapy). (3.33)
That which is called *vājīkaraṇa* (aphrodisiac therapy) increases the seminal essence (*retodhātu*) by means of destroying existing diseases and nourishing the body's limbs. (3/34)
By following the path of Ayurveda, one may arouse the vital essence (rasa) for the sake of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa—so says the Daughter of the Mountain. (3.35)
Even if one were capable in every respect, possessing a body subject to disease, that which is characterized as the self would first perish through illness, like a drop of water. (3/36)
But the gradual diminution of the other ancillaries is now described;
therefore, first, like that of the great enemy, the rasa (of passion). (3.37)
If rasa is destroyed, from where can there be the Self, from where Bhairava the Blissful, and from where the arising of merit through the worship of the Liṅga of Maheśa? (3/38)
Therefore, one should protect the vital essence (*rasa*) through the methods prescribed for longevity and honor oneself with various substances that nourish the semen (*śukla*). (3.39)
Therefore, this compendium of medicine is for the purpose of honoring Anandadeva;
furthermore, this is declared to be the purpose of the science of archery (dhanurveda). (3.40)
A king who is a warrior skilled in the practice of the bow attains the fruit of a sacrifice if he meets death in battle. (3.41)
If the lord of the earth should conquer those who are arrogant or those who are timid,
then, having secured his kingdom, he enjoys the bliss of the Liṅga. (3.42)
Therefore, even the Vedic scripture concerning the bow is intended for the attainment of the bliss of one's own nature;
however, the Gāndharva Veda is a great science, extensively elaborated by Bharata and others. (3.43)

He who pleases virtuous people by both means—through the *tāṇḍava* dances with their exuberant movements as described by me, and through the graceful charms of the *lāsya* dance as described by you—is truly great. (3.44)
Dance, song, and instrumental music—these three are called *saṅgīta* (concerted performance).
Generally, those who possess the essence of *saṅgīta* are said to be masters of sound (*nādaka*). (3.45)

Because of the abundance of those thousands of poetic forms (*rūpaka*) consisting of the nine sentiments (*rasa*) and so forth, the brilliant erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgārarasa*) shall be established. (3.46)
The well-known designation "rasa" for the heroic, the marvelous, and so forth, has been established by those who are deluded;
or else, it is traditionally remembered as "rasa" because they are colored (or permeated) by that [delusion]. (3.47)
Therefore, the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*) is predominant, for it has desire as its life-force;
and that [desire] consists of the sight and touch of a couple who are mutually favorable. (3.48)
This friend is more closely associated than anyone else with the Sound of Universal Bliss;
through the falling away of the self, that Sound is the cause of bliss according to the Śāstra.
Now, the science of polity (*arthaśāstra*) also exists for the sake of delighting in its own characteristic marks;
and that is of two kinds: the *nītiśāstra* of Bṛhaspati and that of Bhārgava. (3.50)
Policy should proceed from the first [means] alone; policy based on the second is demonic.
It is accomplished through the six qualities, the powers, and the three successes. (3.51)
And through three sprinklings and three means, this entire treatise on ethics becomes radiant; it bestows the prosperity of wealth and all forms of abundance. (3.52)
Through the objects perfected by the science of wealth (arthaśāstra), one acquires truth;
this is the third human goal (puruṣārtha), whose nature is the bliss of the Self. (3.53)
Therefore, both political science (nīti) and the art of diplomacy (dṛti) are also promoters of the bliss of enjoyment.
Thus has the essential purport of the eighteen branches of knowledge been correctly declared. (3.54)
O beloved, all philosophical systems (darśanas) have bliss as their ultimate goal;
liberation exists in every scripture, though its specific form differs from one to another. (3.55)

then, with that water, [one should draw] a square and a hexagon in the front portion.
Having drawn a circle, a triangle, and a dot, one should worship the Foundation (Ādhāra). Here, the pure Kalās are to be worshipped with the Ādhāra-mantra.
One should join the vessel with its base using the *pātra* mantra;
then, having worshipped the digits of the Sun, one performs the initial filling.
Having prepared the vessel, the wise one should worship the digits (kalās) of the Moon and the Sun there, having placed the primary and the intermediate [substances] therein. (6.51)
One should draw the city of Fire (Agni) consisting of the vowels and consonants; having written the young girl (Bālā) in the corners, one should draw a hexagon outside.
Having worshipped that hexagon according to the rule with the six-limbed rite,
one should touch the *arghya* water with the nine hundred and four rays beginning with the face of emanation (*sṛṣṭimukha*).
One should consecrate it with the five mantras beginning with "Akhaṇḍa" and also with the root mantra;
thus, by these mantras, the first supreme nectar becomes consecrated.
Freed from all defects and devoid of all impurities,
it becomes the generator of supreme bliss and the sole means for attaining perfection.
One should show the external seven mudrās, beginning with the *trikhaṇḍa-mudrā*, which destroys all sins without exception and consists of the nature of bliss.
Sthāpana, Sannidhāna, Sannirodha, Ava-kuṇṭhana, Vandana, Dhenu, and Yoni—these are proclaimed as the seven mudrās. (6/57)
The wise one should please her with the sixty-four types of offerings;
for each of these sixty-four offerings, there is a separate mantra dedicated to the Goddess. (6.58)
Then, having displayed the nine mudrās, one should worship the heart [of the deity] three times with the root mantra;
likewise, the six limbs with the limb-mantras, and the sixteen Nityās of the lunar days.
And with their respective mantras, numbering seventy-eight (the seven sages and four Vedas),
one who is full of devotion should worship the lineage of the Lords and the feet of one's own guru upon the head.
In the three outer cities of Mahī, within the outer house of Mahī, the powers beginning with *aṇimā* are proclaimed; in the inner house of Mahī, those beginning with Brāhmī are proclaimed. (6/61)
In the meantime, within the house on the ground, one should worship the mudrās, beginning with Saṃkṣobhaṇā,
by offering them to the Yoginīs with the mantra of surrender (samarpaṇa).
Then, one should worship the Mistress of the Wheel named Tripurā with her mantra;
having displayed the Saṃkṣobha mudrā, one should worship the sixteen-spoked [wheel].
There, the digits (kalās) of that treasury of digits, headed by Kāmākarṣiṇī, are to be worshipped as the secret yoginīs; [they are] Tripureśī and Cakriṇī.
The mudrā is declared to be Drāviṇī; thereafter, the wise one should worship the eight-spoked [wheel], wherein the Śaktis beginning with Anaṅgakusumā are stationed.
Those who are the most secret Yoginīs, Cakriṇī and Purasundarī, should be known as the Mudrā Ākarṣiṇī; thereafter, in Bhuvanāraka— (6.66).
One should worship the fourteen principal goddesses who cause universal agitation:
the Saṃpradāya Yoginīs, Tripurā, Śrī, and Cakriṇī.
The mudrā should be known as "subjugated" (vaśīkṛtā); then one should worship the ten-spoked [wheel].
The power (śakti) such as all accomplishments (sarvasiddhi) and so forth is indeed the Yoginī who has transcended the Kula.
And the auspicious Mudronmādakarī resides in Cakriṇīpura;
these goddesses, beginning with Sarvajñā, are proclaimed as the deities of the inner ten-spoked wheel.
These are Garbhayoginī, Cakreśī, Puramālinī, and Mahāṅkuśā; she is the Mudrā in the great enclosure of the eight-spoked wheel.
One should worship Vaśinī and the others, as well as her secret Yoginīs;
Cakriṇī, Tripurā, Siddhā, and Khecarī become the Mudrās. (6.71)
Alternatively, the weapons beginning with the letter *va* should be worshipped through the Weapon-science (*āyudhavidyā*).
In the triangle are Kāmeśvarī, Vajreśvarī, and Bhagamālinī.
Then, in the center, Lalitā should be worshipped by the wise one, as well as Yoginī, Atirahasyā, Tripurāmbā, and Cakriṇī. (6.73)
Then, within the wheel of bliss (*ānandacakra*), which consists of all seeds and is characterized by the form of the drop (*bindu*) and great rapture, one should worship the supreme goddess Lalitā.
O God, she who is known as the supreme secret of the higher and the lower, endowed with the *yonimudrā*,
has her body closely joined with his on a single seat.
Resembling the rising sun, eternally sixteen years of age, possessing the beauty of ten million Cupids, and wielding the flower-arrows and bow. (6.76)
One should worship Kāmeśvara, who holds a noose and a goad and is adorned with ornaments made of all kinds of jewels, by means of the mantra beginning with the letter *ha*.
One should worship Kāmeśī with the mantra beginning with the letter *ka*.
Having thus worshipped the Goddess in nine enclosures according to the prescribed rite, || 6.78 ||
At the conclusion of the incense, lamps, and food offerings, one should display the mudrās in their proper sequence;
then, having recited the Saubhāgyahṛdaya mantra, one should meditate upon Kāmakalā.
One should perform the rite of oblation (*homa*) in the manner that will be described;
then, having satisfied [the deities], one should worship the God and the Goddess with the two root-mantras.
Having attained non-duality with Ānanda, one should contemplate the unity of those two;
when they have become one within the body, one should worship Ānandabhairava. (6.81)

The knower of mantras, having recited the previously mentioned mantra for the Goddess with its six limbs, should satisfy the Lord, the Supreme Ishvara who is the kinsman of bliss, with drops [of nectar]. (6.82)
O Maheśvarī, whether ten times, a hundred times, or a thousand times [the recitation of] this *Yāgarāja-krama* is known by the wise as the *Nāndī-pūjā*. (6.83)
I shall now describe the King of Sacrifices (Yāgarāja) in due order; listen, O beloved! Having heard it, a person who worships with vigor shall attain perfection.
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the Ānandatantra. || 6/6 ||
The Seventh Chapter:
Having performed the *nāndīmukha* rite, one should perform the King of Sacrifices (*yāgarāja*), the procedure for which is difficult even for the Maruts to attain. (7.1)
Hearing it generates merit and cuts away evil;
it is the cause of supreme bliss and good fortune, and bestows all perfections. (7.2)
Even when performed but once, this sacrifice bestows all accomplishments;
however, it is prescribed to be performed every year for the sake of its perfection. (7.3)
O Goddess, if performed every month, it will grant even the state of Śiva; but if performed on the auspicious festival days (parvan), it will grant whatever is desired at any time.
O Īśānī, for the sake of the Great Yoga, trees, shrubs, creepers, and so forth were created by me in the form of Brahmā throughout the three worlds, O fair-hipped one. (7.5)
O Maheśvarī, honey is prepared from the juice of those various powers and medicinal herbs, both individually and collectively.
Having prepared *madana* as prescribed in the scriptures, one should worship with that substance.
All women were created by me for the purpose of honoring the Lord of the Linga (Liṅgeśvara). (7/7)
Among these means of accomplishment, these beautiful-eyed women are the primary objects of worship;
they belong to those of the East, the North, and even the Middle Country. (7.8)
They say this pure body of Kula-śakti is the very essence;
it is perfume, flower, betel, ointment, delight, and medicine. (7.9)
The first, the secondary, the middle, and the fourth,
as well as five others— these fifteen are the means for accomplishing the sacrifice.
Among these, the first five are the principal ones, with Kuleśvarī as the foremost;
even among those, O Dear One, only two are primary—the first and the fifth.
The first entity is the stainless one; the fifth consists of the family powers (kulaśakti).
Janārdana is both the first and the last, being the very essence.
By entering the state of withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*), he whose banner bears the eagle seized [the world] through his eighth incarnation in the form of Baladeva. (7.13)
By the Lord who possesses infinite forms, born from the womb of Rohiṇī, and who bears the burden of supporting the great weight of this earthly sphere.
But the lotus-eyed one proclaimed the very first and essential [portion] of that great, wise god Balabhadra. (7.15)
But there is never a separation from the essence of the first;
it is like the sweet honey from the mouth of Revatī, perfumed by the Bhojas. 7.16
While they drink, the surface of the earth is supported by Balabhadra,
who has been presented by Varuṇa at the command of Kṛṣṇa, the lord of Bala.
The collection of ingredients for wine, which generates strength and increases virility, should be obtained from within the hollow of a *nīpa* tree on the slopes of Mount Gomataparvata. (7.18)
Seeing her, the distressed son of Rohiṇī (Balarāma) drank in all the bliss of the Supreme Goddess, Svānanda, and departed for the protection of the world.

But the Lord, whose eyes are like lotuses, performed the formal reception of the final essence, the substance for the worship of consciousness. (7.21)
Although he was the son of Vasudeva, Sahadeva—the best of the Yadus—assumed the status of Nanda’s son for the purpose of deceiving Kaṃsa. (7.22)
There in Vraja, O fortunate one, were thousands of cowherd girls who were beyond counting—naturally sweet and possessing the conduct of celestial beings. (7.23)
In his own home, the Lord of the World possesses objects for the worship of the family;
yet those cowherd girls, noble in their virtues, were not enjoyed by the Enemy of Mura. (7.24)
There is no place in Vṛndāvana where he has not played; for the sake of his own blissful form and for the purpose of his spiritual perfection, the subduer of Mura has sported there. (7.25)
He performed the sequence of the King of Sacrifices, deluding all people,
while delighting the cowherd girls by playing the flute.
He wore the attire of Madanagopa, rosy as a fresh sprout,
adorned with a bow of sugarcanes and equipped with flowers as his arrows.
Holding a shining noose and a goad,
Kṛṣṇa, who is himself a goad for the wicked, sported in many ways with his various family powers (kulaśaktis).
Thus, in childhood at the cowherd settlement, and later in youth during his reign, even sixteen thousand years were spent by him confined within hell. (7.29)
The lotus-eyed one took another faultless woman as his wife;
furthermore, he was resplendent, enriched by Rukmiṇī, Satyā, and Jāmbavatī.
The great women of the city gathered the group together with the family preceptors;
therefore, there was a primary sense of bliss in the ritual of worshiping the deity. || 7/31 ||
O beloved, even from the very beginning, the Kula-energies (kulaśaktis) are the essence;
O Pārvatī, through every form of worship, there is rest in them alone.
Therefore, this means known as the power of the lineage (kula-śakti) should be accepted, wherein the rays of one's own blissful splendors manifest. (7.33)
Having offered the oblation at the conclusion of the Nāndīmukha rite, the mantra-adept, having paid homage to Maheśānī Mahātripurasundarī, [should proceed]. (7.34)
Having pleased [him] with many sweet hymns, the wise one, bowing low in devotion, performed circumambulations and prostrations. || 7.35 ||
Taking a handful of flowers along with fragrant substances, kuśa grass, and unbroken grains,
one should scatter them at his feet while reciting this mantra and prostrate like a staff.
O Ānandayāga, who produces rest for all and who is beautiful with every kind of bliss, I now perform [this rite]; please show me favor. (7.37)
Having thus obtained permission from the Lord of Gods, the practitioner should rise again and worship his own guru and the guru’s wife three times at the end of each pair of deities.
Then, having invited and summoned a joyful messenger girl adorned with auspicious marks, who is beautiful and belongs to the eight [families] such as the Kula and Akula, [he should proceed]. (7.39)
Having worshipped with fragrant oils consecrated by the Ānaṃdadeva mantra, the wise one should massage every limb.
Having caused him to put on a pure cloth—either reddish or scented—or else a multicolored one, or a beautiful silk garment. (7.41)
Having adorned her even with ornaments—earrings, armlets, and bracelets;
with girdles, anklets, necklaces, single-strand strings, and arm-bands. (7.42)
The wise man, having adorned her with *sīmantasīma*, vermilion, black collyrium, lac, and other ornaments, [should proceed]. (7.43)
One should cause her to sit properly on a seat with soft and thick cotton;
she should not be dispassionate, nor excessively passionate, nor fond of quarreling.
She should not be fierce, arrogant, talkative, or cruel;
she should not speak untruths, nor be attached to others, nor be too corpulent, nor too short, nor too emaciated. (7.45)
Neither too tall nor too dark, neither too high nor too pale; her limbs are not coarse, her eyes are not squinting, and her bones are not rough.
She was not emaciated with visible veins, nor was she stout, nor did she have uneven teeth; she did not behave like a procuress, nor was she devoted to mockery. (7.47)
She is not one who harbors hatred toward the Kaula tradition, nor is she fond of the Cārvāka doctrine;
she is neither foul-smelling, nor of bad character, nor a slanderer. (7.48)
One who is not overcome by thirst, nor afflicted by hunger, thirst, and the like, and whose limbs are not seized by chronic disease, is fit to be a messenger (dūtikā). (7.49)
I shall describe the two-fold purification of the messenger (dūtī), both external and internal;
likewise, there are two purifications for the vital breath (jīva) within the body. (7.50)
There are two for the body and two for Śiva; these purificatory rites (saṃskāras) are of four kinds:
namely, anointing, rubbing with unguents, bathing, and then anointing with ointment. || 7/51 ||
Perfuming the hair, arranging the hair, applying fragrances, wearing soft garments, and the fashioning of barley-shaped figures on cloth. (7.52)
O Daughter of the Mountain, this is the external refinement of the body;
now listen, O long-eyed one, as the internal one is also described for the station of Ānandanātha, which abides in the form of a triangle.
The state of being hairless, translucence, smoothness, and fragrance. || 7/54 ||
O Pārvatī, [it possesses] the state of being well-perfumed, moistness, the internal absorption of liquid water,
extreme softness, purity, and excellent touch.
The soft luster of the interior of a slightly blossomed lotus,
the state of being a parasol of fine silk, and the presence of a waning crescent moon.
O beautiful one, you possess neither excessive coldness nor excessive heat;
you have a natural delicacy of being and a natural fragrance.

The impressioning of the latent tendencies (saṃskāra) occurs instantly; even for one who is moistened, there is a firm stability. It is free from excessive expansion and devoid of extreme contraction. (7.58)
Merely by being touched, she was suddenly filled with the melting flow of passion;
she possessed the capacity to endure the force of enjoyment and was fit to be the object of the eightfold pleasures.
O Pārvatī, the absence of roughness within the skin, a glossy complexion, and the state of being entirely free from violent itching—these are its qualities. (7.60)
Though afflicted by many diseases such as hemorrhoids located in the private parts, he remains untroubled and robust, possessing a strength equal to the rim of a chariot wheel. (7.61)
The state of being like a leaf of the *aśvattha* tree, the condition of being a jewel that has not yet emerged, similarity to the head of a serpent, and likewise a state of clear fluidity. (7.62)
She possesses the likeness of the mouth of a very affectionate kalaviṅka bird immediately after birth;
she is endowed with all auspicious marks and is devoid of any marks of low lineage. (7.63)
Such qualities as these have been declared for the female messenger (dūtī) in the abode of Smara;
O beloved, those qualities shine forth through the very power of refinement (saṃskāra).
Therefore, O beloved, refinement is not at all appropriate for a messenger;
yet even refinement should apply to all matters. (7.65)
But the refined (*saṃskṛta*) place of the vulva (*bhaga*), O Daughter of the Mountain, belongs to the female messenger (*dūtī*);
it generates all good fortune and is the great seat of all accomplishments (*siddhi*). (7.66)
It brings joy to all, effects liberation for all, and is the means for the worship of Ānandabhairava, which deludes the entire universe. (7.67)
It bestows delight upon heroes of great majesty who are rich in virtues;
it possesses most beautiful feet and jaws, and it utterly cuts away all afflictions.
It is the abode of the power of bliss, the playground of the bodiless god of love,
the dwelling place of the crescent moons, and the home of the wealth of all auspicious fortunes.
The seat of the vulva of the Unconditioned (asaṃskṛta-bhaga) is the promoter of extreme evil;
it generates all diseases and brings about misfortune. (7/70)
It causes the torment of the afflictions of hell, brings about a miserable state of existence, generates public reproach, and incurs the world's censure. (7.71)
It is offensive at first sight, foul-smelling, smelling of urine, and full of impurities;
it is frothy, putrid, leavings of food, degraded, and smeared with filth. (7.72)
It is hairy, censured by the world, and contemptible to those who observe the proper times;
it is internally rich with tough skin and endowed within with a tongue.
With an interior as hard as a wooden pin, its skin thickened by rough calluses,
and abounding with scabies and itching, such a most wicked ulcer is described as "liquid" (drava).
The vulva of the messenger (dūtī) arises from the state of being unconditioned;
therefore, the construction of its refinement must be performed by the practitioners of yoga (yoginīs).
What greater fortune could there be than this, that [the vulva], though naturally defiled by impurity, [is thus purified]?
Indeed, that very body of one's own is intended as the means for worship.
Therefore, in the pavilion of the abode of passion, the well-refined messenger (dūtī) brings forth the Supreme One in person, who assumes the form of non-dual bliss. (7.77)
Thus, this section on refinement has been clearly explained regarding the Bhaga; now, O beautiful lady, listen as the refinement of the mouth of the messenger (dūtī) is described. (7.78)
The grinding of uneven teeth with the edge of a blade, the sharpening with a weapon, and the subsequent polishing to make them stainless; (7.79)
By applying the ash of burnt betel nut along with camphor to the teeth, they become very smooth; and by gargling with oil, a luster is produced in the teeth. (7.80)
The water of a coconut fruit is exceedingly delightful when used as a mouth-rinse.
[One may also use] the three pungents (trikaṭu), the three myrobalans (triphalā), māṃsī, jaggery, cinnamon bark, leaves, and filaments. 7/81.
Having ground together *tālīsa* and sandalwood with coconut water, one should form pills the size of an axle-pin;
first, the female messenger (*dūtī*) should swallow one of them.
By that, there shall be the pacification of all phlegm situated in the throat that causes foul odors, as well as of all impurities that have been discharged. (7.83)
The wise man should also grind musk with camphor and the twigs of the khadira tree with great care, and fashion them into the form of pills.
Having chewed the betel leaf together with him three or four times, she should prepare his mouth, which smells of rot, so that it possesses fragrance. (7.85)
Thus, O Mistress of the Kula, the purification of the mouth has been described;
in this manner, the external and internal purification of the body has been proclaimed. (7.86)
48k) Now, O Goddess, I shall describe the external and internal refinement (saṃskāra) of that messenger (dūtī), who exists as his very life-soul (jīvātman). || 7/87 ||
Even the messenger and the Lord of Life, though augmented as if by the impurity of beginningless ignorance, are worthy of the supreme consecration.
O daughter of the mountain, behold the haughty behavior of the impurities,
since she sports fearlessly even in the presence of Śiva, who is called the individual soul (jīva) and is devoid of attachment.
All the activities of the scriptures are for the purpose of removing impurities;
[they concern] the Great Lord known as one's own life-force, who is obscured by the ignorance of primordial sound (nāda).
All the sequences of worship do not produce the divine nature of the one whose form is the individual soul; rather, they serve to remove impurities. (7.91)
O Śivā, if the impurity of the messenger’s life is not removed, then even one's own pure self may become defiled through the power of that association. (7.92)
It is certain that virtues and defects arise quite differently from association;
the hearing of her [the Vedic tradition’s] time is proclaimed as the first [requirement]. (7.93)
The three principles, purification, and the instruction on the vidyās are accomplished by means of a mantra of few syllables that effects the burning away of the fetters.
The awakening to the path of peace is achieved through effortless training;
it arises neither from passion, nor from greed, nor from the great delusion. (7.95)
The honoring of women should be performed in accordance with the scriptures alone;
for women, whose minds are by nature simple, do not understand the ultimate truth. (7.96)
"Listen, O messenger, hear this discourse on reality from me: women are by nature fickle, and their pride is inherently inexhaustible. (7.97)
Exhilarated by the intoxication of youth— which lasts but a few days and resembles a swelling river— her breasts were seen to be heaving.
He regards what should be done as if it were not to be done, and what should not be done as if it were to be done;
he has no trust in anyone at all, nor does he place confidence in the words of his preceptor. (7.99)
Impetuosity is always and eternally attached to the mind;
these are known as the confluence of tens of thousands of faults.
According to the vision of the scriptures, one's own worship is caused solely by one's own passion.
Women who consider themselves to be of bad conduct fall into hell.
Just as there may be an accomplishment of worship through auspicious perfumes, flowers, garlands, betel, unguents, clothing, and mouth-perfume; || 7/102 ||
The first, the second, the middle one, and the fourth—all this is accomplished through the worship of Maheśa, as prescribed. (7.103)
Thus, by our own good fortune resulting from the meritorious deeds performed in previous lives, this humble body of ours has been made fit for the wise to employ as a means of worship. (7.104)
Therefore, having attained her purpose, that bride considers herself as one who has been led by the high-souled practitioner to the supreme worlds beyond the *sāla* trees. (7.105)
In the world of Brahmā, in the world of Truth, or even in the abode of the gods,
in the world of Viṣṇu, or in the world of Rudra, they sport with manifold delights.
Seated before the lion throne, she becomes my chief servant;
listen to me for the entirety of the Dharma, if you desire such good fortune. (7.107)
"O messenger, for the sake of worship, you shall not attain a good rebirth"—with such words, joined with reasoning and consistent with the scriptures, [he spoke]. (7.108)
The messenger (dūtī) of Jīvanātha should perform the external consecration (saṃskāra).
Thus, having her limbs purified by the consecrations, seated comfortably upon a seat,
one should meditate upon the messenger as the Goddess Ānandabhairavī herself.
The practitioner should also invoke Ānandabhairavī with the mantra.
Having worshipped with the fivefold offerings (pañcopacāra), one should satisfy [the deities] with drops of nectar (ali-bindu).
Furthermore, Rati, Prīti, and Manobhava, situated within the triangle, should be worshipped again.
At the base of the pentagon, however, are the deities beginning with Drāviṇī:
Drāviṇī, Śoṣiṇī, Bandhinī, and likewise Mohinī.
And Unmādinī—these five are the deities of the arrows of the Mind-born;
they are to be worshipped in the moving five-spoked [yantra], along with Kāmarāja-Umaheśvarī (or Kāmarāja-Maleśvarī).
Kaṃdarpa, Manmatha, Makaraketana, Manobhava, and Pañcama—these are the five who cause agitation to the world. (7.114)
Then, on the eight petals, the eight Anaṅga-śaktis, who possess the color of the rising sun and hold bows and arrows, should be worshipped by the wise.
Anaṅgakusumā and Anaṅgamekhalā were the second;
along with Anaṅgamadanā and Anaṅgamadanāturā. (7.116)
Anaṅgarekhā, Anaṅgavegā, Anaṅgākuśā,
and Anaṅgamālinī— these eight should be worshipped according to the prescribed rite.
Having thus worshipped it, one should contemplate that which resides within the radiant lotus of the heart—
the wheel of bliss (ānandacakra), which increases the tumultuous roar of joy.
By the rays of desire, intensely crimson as they emerge from the bodies of the deities of those wheels,
shimmering with a yellowish glow like the brilliance of lightning.
One should contemplate her entire network of channels (*nāḍīcakra*) as agitated;
[one should contemplate] the fresh [nectar] flowing from the channels due to the arousal of the power of Anaṅga. (7.120)
A single continuous flow has arisen, mixed with essence and blood;
it is filled with the flood of the river of passion, full of redness, and intensely crimson. (7.121)
It generates total bliss, bestows rest to the mind,
and is permeated by a flood of melting passion through the discernment of its various meanings.
Having led [the worshipper] to the place of Candrakalā, one should worship the Yonicakra.
The Śrīdevī said: "O Śaṅkara, who is this named Candrakalā, and where does she reside? (7.123)
"What is its form, what is its nature, and what is its color? Tell me this.
Śrī Kāmeśvara replied: "Listen; that which is named Kāmakalā is the channel that carries the waters of the serpent's coils."
O Śāṅkarī, her pervasion exists throughout all the channels;
and the entire wheel of channels, O fair-faced one, is pervaded by her. (7.125)
In the body, certain channels are said to carry the vital breath (prāṇa);
some carry blood, and some carry enthusiasm (utsāha).
Some carry nutritional essence (rasa), and some carry dejection (dainya).
Some are carriers of bliss, while one alone is a carrier of impurity.
One channel carries urine; some carry the objects of the senses;
eight carry the waters of enjoyment, and among them, the supreme is the digit of the moon (caṇdrakalā).
The first is called Candrakalā, the second is Candracandrikā; then there are Candrarekhā, Candravatī, and Candramahodayā. (7.129)
Candriṇī, Candragarbhā, Candronmattā, and likewise Aṣṭamī—these are the clouds of enjoyment, supported by the digits of the moon through their own portions. (7.130)
Enveloped by those channels that carry the waters of enjoyment,
she is the primary element, possessing a radiance equal to a flash of shimmering lightning.
Her inner being was overflowing with the intense liquefaction of passion;
she took her seat upon the navel-cakra, which is the root of all the channels (nāḍīs).
The channel called Candrakalā has been declared to be the increaser of all good fortune;
O Supreme Goddess, its opening by means of the mouth is difficult to attain in this world. (7.133)
Through many extremely rigorous austerities performed in previous births,
such a person may be born among a thousand Kaulas, perhaps only two or three in number.
If one’s linga is sprinkled even once in this life with the subtle drops of semen falling from that channel of the dissolved Ananga, [he attains perfection]. (7.135)

He who is the Great Lord of Bliss among the gods and the wives of the gods;
