And that which resides within the respective powers of the Dānavas and Daityas—may I bring that very bliss here for the sake of attaining the perfection of my own true nature. (9.39)
I shall bring here this bliss, which is established within the very nature of the self, from the powers such as Śacī belonging to Indra and the other guardians of the world.
May that which resides within the powers of the seven sages, headed by Marīci and Atri,
bring this bliss here for the sake of perfecting my own true nature.
I shall bring here that bliss which shines within Brahmā, Sarasvatī, and even Sāvitrī, for the sake of perfecting the true nature of the Self.
I bring here this bliss which exists in Viṣṇu, in Kamalā, and also in Bhūdevī, for the sake of perfecting the realization of one's own true nature.
May he who has established his abode in the mind of Umāpati and in Umā herself bring here this bliss for the sake of attaining the realization of the true nature of the Self. (9.44)
The bliss belonging to the Lord of Desire resides within the Mistress of Desire;
for the sake of perfecting the nature of the Self, I shall bring that bliss here.
By food everything is born, and by food alone it grows;
therefore, one should lead the sheath composed of food to the state of being composed of bliss. (9.46)
The vital breaths (prāṇas) are said to be the life-force; indeed, everyone moves by means of the vital breaths.
Therefore, one should lead the sheath consisting of vital breath (prāṇamaya), which is crying out, to the state of being the sheath of bliss (ānandamaya). (9.47)
The mind touches upon actions; the mind alone is the lord of the bull.
Therefore, one should lead the sheath consisting of the mind to the state of being composed of bliss.
The entire form of consciousness is established within consciousness;
one should lead that sheath consisting of consciousness to the state of bliss.
Bliss is life itself; bliss is the Supreme Lord.
May that sheath consisting of bliss increase, increase for me! 9.50
The wise man, reciting the *Ānandakārikā*, should gradually lead his entire youthful exuberance toward the performance of the sacrificial rite. (9.51)
The gestures and the sources of erotic passion that have been taught by me in the Ratitantra—all of those, O lady of beautiful hips, attain the state of being limbs here in this [tantra]. (9.52)
In the Smarāgama, these are described in various distinct ways;
who in this world is capable of describing their countless varieties? (9.53)
And one should perform that entire web of ritual actions upon the messenger (dūtī);
through all of these, the Great Lord, who is the bliss of one's own self, attains manifestation. (9.54)
Through various kinds of embraces, kisses, bites, diverse scratching with the nails, agitations, and acts of endearment; (9.55)
Through playful anger artfully contrived as endearments, through sequences of talk about her beloved, through the "curu-curū" sounds of joy at her ear, and through the kissing of her eyes; || 9.56 ||
[The embrace] consists of slaps upon the navel, the paths of the fingernails, the sprouts of the nails, the pressing of the breasts, and even the lifting up of the armpits. (9.57)
With the lapping of their tongues against their palates and the whistling sounds from their palate-tips, there were the cries of crows, *kāraṇḍava* ducks, cranes, and other birds. (9.58)
O Pārvatī, there were swans with eyes like jasmine, and pigeons,
emitting various kinds of sweet warbling sounds from their throats.
By whirling above and below, by hurling them down from on high, by seizing them by the hair, by blows with the hands, and by many duels with the tongues; (9.60)
With encouragements, with pleasing words, with tokens of affection, and with praises for her skill in love and her good fortune at every step. (9.61)
She should delight the female messenger by means of smiles, clever conversations, and other various kinds of gestures in many different ways. (9.62)

Just as the *prayāja*, *anuyāja*, and other rites attain the status of auxiliary limbs (*aṅga*) in a sacrifice, so too shall the embrace and other acts become auxiliary limbs in this sacrifice of bliss. (9.63)
The two breasts of the messenger girl serve as the sacrificial posts, her hair becomes the grass-strewing, the glowing fire of nail-marks is present, and the kiss is like the drinking of Soma. (9.64)
The pair of arms are the *sruva* and *upabhṛt* ladles; the base of the arm is called the *juhū* ladle.
The sprinkling of water is the sweat-fluid, and the surrounding covering is the *paristṛti*. || 9/65 ||
The lower garment is the movement [of breath], and the sacrificial altar is the middle region;
the navel-cavity is the *cātvāla*, and the *gārhapatya* fire is known as the mouth. (9.66)
The Dakṣiṇāgni fire is her chin, the Maṇḍala fire is her hand-palms,
and the Sabhya and Āvasathya fires are situated on her two sides.
The Āhavanīya fire itself would be the moist temple of Madana;
the friction of the fuel-sticks is said to be the oblation, and Maheśvara is the Liṅga, the offerer. (9.68)
The sacrificer is supreme bliss; the Udgātṛ is the sound of humming;
the Adhvaryu is the hissing sound; and the Neṣṭṛ is sweet speech.
The Prastotṛ is the commencement of the song, the Pratihartṛ is its rising;
the Maitrāvaruṇa is enthusiasm, and the Potṛ is said to be the syllable *huṃ*. (9.70)

The Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin priest performed the shaking; the Brahman priest engaged in confused movements; the Acchāvāka priest uttered a croaking sound; and there was the great oblation of the Śukla-Indra sacrifice.

The sense organs are the members of the assembly; this is called the Great Sacrifice (mahāyāga). Having slain the sacrificial animal—which is the very nature of bliss—the Great Goddess [attains her state]. (9.72)
From the preparation of that sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa), the great sacrifice proceeds.
The Illustrious Goddess said: "O Śaṅkara, [even] by nail-scratches, tooth-bites, and even blows... (9.73)
"O Lord, what is accomplished by these violent agitations and even by the forceful descents?
Tell us their purpose; otherwise, these actions would be fruitless. (9.74)
O Hero, for what purpose is that which is performed upon the breasts of the messenger (dūtī) ordained? O Lord, tell me the reason for that action, beginning with the striking. (9/75)

"O Lord of Desire, you have asked well this question. Those who are intoxicated by the madness of their own nature experience delusion moment by moment through the messenger girl during amorous play. (9.76)
In the assembly of those bewildered by delusion, whose activities consist of the enjoyment of fine garments, the female messengers have become sluggish and do not move at all. (9.77)
The god of love, having reached a state of stillness within their minds, lingers in order to grant them pleasure; for how can there be happiness without that lingering? (9.78)
Because they do not manifest themselves, there would be an obstacle to the sacrifice of sexual union;
therefore, once awakened, they exert themselves with enthusiasm in the rite of passion. (9.79)
Thus cherished by various kinds of heroes through their diverse deeds, the messenger runs forth repeatedly like butter melting in the fire. (9.80)
One should construct the machine of yoga; all this constitutes the cluster of ritual actions.
Then, O Dear One, there is the dissolution (laya), the dissolution of objects (arthalaya), and also the dissolution of the pivot (ghaṭṭalaya).
Agitation and whirling shall occur sequentially by means of the *liṅga*;
moving through the body of the messenger (*dūtī*), one should lead it to a state consisting of bliss. (9.82)
The wise one, his own self being exceedingly steadfast, softens her by means of various ritual services while contemplating the key of the *liṅga*.
Restraining the outward flow of the flickering rasa within,
one should contemplate that reality consisting of eternal bliss which pervades the entire universe.
This alone is the worship of the Guru; this is remembered as the adoration of Śiva.
This alone is the great sacrifice, and this is the unsurpassed austerity. (9.85)
O deities, when you attain satisfaction through the joy found herein, this vow—which is of great merit—bestows the non-duality of bliss. (9.86)
Thus, gradually expanding the heroic great sacrifice (vīramahāyāga),
one should act so that the seminal essence (bindu) does not fall and the mind remains joyful.
One should perform the ritual action in such a way that the messenger flows;
the emission of the drop is called the final ablution of the sacrifice.
Even this principal oblation ought not to be performed in the middle;
rather, it should be done with increasing firmness as the duration of time grows longer. (9.89)
One should perform the great sacrifice (mahāyāga) in that manner for the sake of perfecting bliss.
Thus ends the ninth chapter in the Ānandatantra.
The Tenth Chapter.
The Holy Goddess said: O Maheśvara, how is it that the drop (bindu) does not leak during union with the womb?
Like mercury in the mouth, fire does not pursue steadfastness. || 10.1 ||
O Caṇḍīśa, how does that which is extremely tremulous, clear, and surrounded by flickering movement become rigid and white within the body? 10.2
O destroyer of worldly existence, you must explain the means for this, if the retention of the white [syllable] produces such extreme wonder. (10.3)
The restraint of the vital breath is appropriate, as is the piercing of the space;
yet the concentration on the white [light] does not arise even with the greatest effort. (10.4)
O Īśānī, this back [of the teaching] has been asked by you; it shall now be explained in detail according to its place—that which has been practiced by many enjoyers in the Kāma-tantras. (10.5)
O highly fortunate lady, I shall describe that which produces great wonder and is difficult to find in the three worlds: the stabilization of the perfection of mercury.
The entire span of time is stilled, and youth is stretched out by men;
yet, somehow, the singular chest of the mature woman is celebrated by the wise. (10.7)
"O beloved, O Goddess, all the minerals, which are extremely fickle and possess extreme velocity, have each taken refuge in their own respective places. (10.8)
This seventh element is not known anywhere by the name of "rasa" (taste); this eternal [element] is all-pervasive and unrestrained. Manifested by foods, it is not, however, produced by food.
Although the Lord of Taste (Raseśvara) dwells within all the networks of channels (nāḍīcakra), [he remains hidden].
Entirely unattached, he sports with absolute independence everywhere;
some say [he dwells] between the eyebrows, others in the heart, and others in the supreme jewel (the *bindu*).
Some, O Goddess, are within the boundary of their own abode; some are within the sphere of food; some are beneath the soles of the feet; and some are at the limit of the hips.
Some say its location is in the waist; some, in the Liṅga-Maheśvara;
others say it is in the mind, while still others have declared it to be in the vital breath (prāṇa).
Even regarding the five senses, there are various delusions of reasoning; these doctrines are unattractive when subjected to critical inquiry. (10.14)
O Mother, listen to that truth which has been told by me:
it resides in the union of the mind and the vital breath, supported by spiritual vigor.
The union of the heart and the vital breath must be accomplished by one who desires the retention of virility;
and for the sake of that union, this Yoga-tantra has been composed by me. (10.16)
The Lord is capable of restraining and sustaining his vigor, pervading it throughout his body,
and uniting it with the *rajas* through the opening of the door of the intellect and the vital winds.
Although many means for the preservation of vigor have been proclaimed, there is no end to them, and through them, the fruit indeed cannot be attained. (10.18)
By means of various smears upon the *liṅga* and various bindings with herbs,
through fierce powers and the sweetness of honey, each subsequent [practice] is superior to the one preceding it.

The maintenance of the pure [state] is not difficult to attain for long, provided one possesses the strength born from contact with the *gaulī* and has a mind whose nature is fixed through the dissolution of the vital breaths (*dhī-maru-dghaṭana*). 10/20.
O auspicious lady, when the means exists, there is indeed no doubt regarding the binding of the pure [soul];
yet, when the heart-abode is present, there is further application.
Indeed, the abandonment of the "cow-dung" (gauḍī) style will not accomplish that particular task;
therefore, the wise person should employ the "cow's urine" (gaur̤ī-vāyu-ta-ghaṭā) style for that purpose.
For those who practice it, the name "anitya" (transient/impermanent) may indeed apply.
Even a slight connection with the wind is not at all the cause of its movement. || 10/23 ||
O Pārvatī, that *gaulī* accomplishes the task together with it;
therefore, the union of the mind and the vital breath (*marut*) is taught first. (10.24)

That Tantra has been proclaimed in many ways by the one who bore the form of Pādāñjali; or rather, that [Tantra] which belongs to the Creator (Brahmā) in its yoga would be difficult to obtain. || 10.25 ||
This tantra was expanded by Yājñavalkya and other yogis through the resonance of the *pādāñjali*, and by Goraikṣa and others through the inner sounds (*nāda*). 10.26.
Their limbs concealed by the power of yoga (yogamāyā) and joined by yoginīs,
their virility rendered motionless through yoga, they constantly enjoy worldly pleasures.
Ādinātha first, followed by the one named Udayana;
then Matsyendra, Nāgorakṣa, Caturaṅgī, and Kandalī. (10.28)
Koṅkaṇeśa, Uruṇagiri, Jalandha, Bhāgavardhana, Capeṭika, Cūḍabāla, and likewise Gobāla (or Gopāla). || 10/29 ||
Muddāyirevaṇa, as well as Rāma and Nāgārjuna; also the one named Vyāla and Heramba, and another known as Śūrpapāyin. || 10.30 ||
Siddhakukkurapāyin and likewise another, the first Lord—by these Maruts, the Ghaṭṭa capable of drawing forth Time (Kālasaṃkarṣaṇa) was established. 10.31.
Others also, their limbs satisfied by having attained the nectar of immortality, wander about;
having shattered the staff of Time, they move through the cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍas).
Among the various divergent paths of thought held by all those perfected ones (siddhas), this doctrine is declared as their very essence for the purpose of preserving that potency. (10.33)
That which is the absolute union of wisdom and means, like water and milk, that very state the yogis declare to be the supreme yoga.
Both of these are like elephants in rut; both of these possess great strength;
both are the creators of the world, being the lords of the mind and the vital breath.
Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna were preeminent and difficult to restrain, like Bhārata and others;
they possessed the wealth of their true nature, which was the light of great consciousness.
Both of them, whose mature power and prowess were mutually superior,
destroyed each other's bodies as they engaged in succession.
When both of these are thoroughly cultivated, they make the living being immortal;
yet when these two are devoid of life, they become like death itself. (10.38)
O beloved, those two worlds consisting of happiness are indeed the worlds of evil; those two worlds consisting of suffering are the worlds of merit.
Those two worlds consisting of evil are indeed the worlds of happiness; those two worlds consisting of merit are the worlds of suffering. (10.39)
O Pārvatī, these two alone are the subtle elements, all-pervasive, and they are the wind of the mind; what is the use of saying more here? (10.40)
The lintel is the door of bliss, and the two keys are for opening the jar; I shall describe their conjunction—listen attentively, O beloved. (10.41)
O Mother, one should drink sixteen measures of air through the *iḍā* [left nostril];
then, with sixty-four measures, one should fill the Lord of Air (*māruteśvara*).
One should exhale through the path of Piṅgalā by means of the thirty-two Mātṛkās;
the duration of the pronunciation of five short syllables is said to be one Mātrā. (10.43)
One should fix the mind on the wind and fill the wind itself;
O Maheśvarī, there are the inhalation (pūraka), the retention (kumbhaka), and the exhalation (recaka).
Sūryaja, Śītala, Hastā, Bhramarī, Kākolakamukha, Vāyupūraṇa, and Bhadrajā; || 10/45 ||
One should exhale the breath when it is properly regulated, fill it when it is properly regulated, and retain it when it is properly regulated;
thus, O God, one shall attain perfection.
The gradual filling of the breath, its gradual restraint, and its gradual release again—by these means, mastery over the vital air is achieved. (10.47)
The wind is exceedingly powerful; it draws everything from all sides and pervades the entire body, acting like a bringer of pleasure when brought under control.
But for one who has not mastered the breath, there is only suffering at every step, despite all the means employed here for the practice of breath-restraint. (10.49)
80k) O beloved, now I shall proclaim the powerful means; listen!
They are: the vision at the door, the awakening of reflective awareness, and also the running. (10.50)
When one directs the wandering gaze toward the meeting point of the mind and the vital air (vāyu), these states arise; at that time, mastery over the vital air is attained. (10.51)
If the practitioner’s vision is always directed toward the movement of the intellect, then the wind, having abandoned its state of enmity, seeks friendship. (10.52)
This body, O fair-hipped one, is a great house with nine doors;
this living soul becomes the householder, with consciousness as his courtyard. (10.53)
The householder, for whom Māyā is his great wealth to be guarded, seeks the end of causes like a thief who hides his measured form within the wind.
Having fashioned a false friendship with his intellect, the Marut moves about both outside and within;
striking at his vulnerabilities, he then strives to seize his life-span and wealth. (10.55)
This friendliness toward all living beings lasts for as long as their life and breath; however, true friendliness belongs to yogis who have attained mastery over the mind and vital energy.
For the world is a friend who is intent on striking at one's vulnerabilities;
therefore, this thief-like wind must be guarded against with great effort. (10.57)
The wind-thief fearlessly enters within and rushes outside, guarding his own body-house through deceit. (10.58)
In this very way, after a few days, the thief who delights in darkness, perceiving the negligence of the mind, sometimes plunders the day.
An external thief who has arrived must be guarded against by men; however, one who is a thief by nature cuts away everything along with its very roots. (10.60)
One who is falsely disciplined, falsely trusting, deceitful, and treacherous—
a thief by nature within— is worthy of punishment for his innate disposition.
Therefore, for the sake of sustaining this vital breath as it flows constantly,
one must strive not to release it, just as one would carefully preserve a supreme goal once attained.
Even a thief must be apprehended after careful observation at every step, he without whom the performance of one's domestic duties cannot be accomplished. (10.63)
If, indeed, some wealth belonging to the house remains within the mind's home, and one goes out without noticing it, then a thief desires to seize it. (10.64)
Therefore, if he perceives the conduct of this very thief,
then that Vāyu and the thief will in time attain friendship.
When such friendship has been established, O Pārvatī, even he— the Wind— [will do so].
He himself proceeds to protect the wealth of his lifespan. || 10/66 ||
When even a thief by nature feels affection for someone anywhere, he seeks to accomplish that person's welfare even at the cost of his own life. (10.67)
Therefore, O Ambika, one should constantly practice the observation of the movement of the mind;
by that means, the mastery of the sound of the vital breath (mārutanāda) is achieved.
Having abandoned excessive distraction, as well as delusion and the vital breath (samīraṇa), one should become of a single flavor with the mind and further attain absorption in That. (10.69)

O lady of beautiful hips, if you desire the accomplishment of yoga without effort, one should bring others under control with a steady gaze, provided one’s intention is not directed elsewhere. (10.70)
When the mind moves, it moves; when the mind stays still, it stays still. Having become like the wind, it bestows the accomplishment of one's purpose. (10.71)
When the wind moves, it moves; when the wind stands still, it stands still.
The mind that has attained identity with that [wind] bestows the gateway to supernatural accomplishment. (10.72)
Upon the destruction of this, the other is surely destroyed; of this there is no doubt.
O Maheśvarī, from the activity of this, the activity of the other arises.
When agitation arises in one [of the senses], it draws upon the agitation of the others;
for the destruction of the mind-wind (*manomāruta*) is indeed the state of being devoid of its restraint. (10.74)
O Daughter of the Mountain, through the practice of long-term cultivation, he attains perfection;
for wherever the mind flows forth, there the vital breath (vāyu) rushes after it. (10.75)
Wherever the vital breath (marut) rushes, there follows the unsurpassed white [element]; by this mind, a drop is led along the paths and the dry grounds.
Like a friendship with the wind, wherever it rushes, there the drop follows after it, exceedingly tremulous; of this there is no doubt. (10.77)
Like a cow running after her calf, she pursues the wind;
yet, O Lord of my mind, she steadies even that which is flickeringly white.
Mutually supporting one another and mutually assisting each other, they both restrain the Lord of Taste (Raseśvara) for the purpose of maintaining life. (10.79)

If the vital drop (*prāṇabindu*) is not present, the vital breaths (*sava*) do not become stable; O Pārvatī, when it possesses the drop, the vital energy becomes firm and life itself becomes stabilized. (10.80)
Longevity, enthusiasm, exhilaration, the joy of knowledge, great strength, luster, nourishment, and contentment are all established in the Lord of the Tongue (Mercury). (10.81)
When the *rasa* dissolves, all that dissolves as well; of this there is no doubt.
But when the *rasa* reaches a state of stillness (*stabdhatām*), O Mother, all that becomes still.
The *rasanā* is indeed the final release, like the *avabhṛtha* bath at the conclusion of a sacrifice;
it is performed by the wise at the end of the eight oblations for the sake of the fruit. (10.83)

As long as the sequence of eight oblations has not been completed in the fire of the liṅga, there shall be the destruction resulting from the interruption of the sacrifice during the offering of food.
Therefore, O Daughter of the Lord of Mountains, having first performed the mental striking with the mace,
one should afterwards effect the nourishment of the body with morsels of food.
The great yoga of the Gaulīs is prepared with substances such as *gulā* and others;
it is an exceedingly powerful consumer of wind (vital energy) and increases mental fortitude. (10.86)
When combined with various kinds of non-essential substances and processed as decoctions, and subjected to intense heating from below, [the essence] becomes greatly increased. (10.87)
When the vessel is joined according to the prescribed method, the *gaulikā* is attained through the medicinal-smoke-filled tube of the apparatus. (10.88)
I shall describe the examination of that; listen attentively, O beloved.
When cloth is smeared with it, fire blazes intensely upon a vessel or similar surface. (10.89)
Even clothing and other such items would not burn when placed in a blazing fire;
therefore, it is exceedingly light, pure, and a destroyer of all diseases and poisons.
It pacifies disorders of phlegm, cures elephantiasis and jaundice, possesses the luster of the sun, sustains the vital breath (anila), maintains fortitude, and increases mental steadfastness. (10.91)
The messenger Drāṇiṇī causes the semen from the womb to be arrested;
she is to be constantly worshipped by those who perform the great sacrifice (mahāyāga). || 10.92 ||
The *gaulī* [vow], endowed with the essence of the tongue, and the *sattva*, *umāna*, and *samāruta* [vows], even up to the limit of eight times eight, the *bindu* brings under control. (10.93)
By this practice of breath-control and through fortitude, even those who are distracted [are steadied];
for, due to the potency of the essence of the *gaulīra* plant, the power of the daughter of the Mountain became paralyzed.
When the pillar has been established through the union of the lord of mercury (rasendra), the fire (dhī), air (marut), and the bull (gauli),
the primary limb of the King of Sacrifices is obtained through the sequence of the desired oblations.
This yoga, which accomplishes the maintenance of vigor, has been explained to you.
O auspicious lady, what else is your mind longing to ask? (10.96)
Wherever there is complete burning, O fair-browed one, there [the state] is discerned.
Thus ends the tenth chapter in the Ānandatantra.
The eleventh chapter. The Goddess said: "O Lord, the sequence of the eight oblations has been revealed as it was indicated."
O Bhavānī, crest-jewel of the moon, please describe his true nature.
The Lord of Desire,
who arises from eight oblations offered by the Goddess through easily accessible and not excessive austerities—
he of great magnanimity performs those eight oblations without deficiency. (11.2)
In the eighth day of the first fortnight (ekāṣṭakā), there shall be good fortune; in the eighth day of the second fortnight (dvyaṣṭama), great fame;
and the oblations offered on the three eighth days (tryaṣṭakā) truly accomplish the conquest of the three worlds for a man.

In this manner, those who offer meritorious oblations into the blazing fire of the Liṅga, beginning with the auspicious Aṣṭakā festival and continuing until its conclusion, [attain great merit]. (11.4)
For them, liberation is held in the palm of their hand; for them, enjoyment is at every step;
and for them, their entire sovereignty is accomplished by mere volition. (11.5)
O Dear One, beginning from the Ekāṣṭakā up to the Aṣṭāṣṭakā,
each subsequent one among these serves as a cause for the bliss of nirvāṇa.
At the conclusion of the single group of eight, however, there is the great sacrifice of the Great Lord;
one should perform it with a single messenger (dūtī), and in a group of eight, with two messengers.
Thus, when the eight groups of eight have been completed, the pinnacle of sacrifice is reached;
the eight messengers (dūtīs) must then be ritually enacted and worshipped according to the true principle.
O Mother, the very sequence that is being described by me regarding the offerings of the Ekāṣṭakā should be inferred, in due order, for the Dvyaṣṭakā and the others as well. (11.9)
O lady of beautiful hips, for one who does not know the true nature of the oblations and their source as they fall from the tip of the ladle, all his various manifestations of power are in vain.
Above the six-fingered cleft of the messenger’s womb,
there exists a captivating vessel of channels named Anaṅgamaṇi.
Resorting to this, one stream has set forth, shining with the splendor of the moon and lotus;
she is renowned as Dinīcī, the self-controlled one who bestows the power of speech.
86k) She exists in the form of the perfection of *aṇimā*, blazing like lightning, through the expansive union with the Great Lord in the form of the *sādhuliṅga*. 11/13.
She stretches out her face and emits a flow of intoxicating fluid;
she possesses a luster dark as the *tāla* tree, yet is slightly reddened by astringent dye.
O fair-browed one, the river born of the Sahya mountains is proclaimed to be slightly slimy;
she is celebrated as the most distinguished among all the great rivers.
He who satiates the fire of the linga with the ladle-mouth of the womb, using the vessel of nectar overflowing from the moon, attains omniscience.
He makes the reality of the elements his own, which is presided over by all;
and having made the reality of the elements his own, he attains a movement that is unimpeded everywhere. (11.17)
Constantly composed, he moves by means of the power of yoga through mountains, trees, walls, and desert lands.
O Great Liṅga, O Maheśāna, I worship your body with the liquified nectar overflowing from the moon; therefore, grant me spiritual perfection.
With this mantra, while embracing his beloved, one should worship the Lord’s liṅga with the fire; this is the first oblation offered by me.
O lotus-eyed one, above that Candronmattā, at a distance of one and a quarter finger-breadths,
there is a certain channel called Candragarbha.
Know that her body, slender like the awn of wild rice and lovely with its golden hue, is the very nectar of that place, which bestows the prosperity of the realization of Kāmeśvarī. (11.22)
O beloved, that which consists of the Tuṅgabhadrā river produces the perfection of greatness;
it is slightly pale-red in color and possesses a fragrance equal to that of the yūthikā jasmine.
He who shall satiate the fire of the *liṅga* with that nectar will, having attained his own state, bring the clouds under his control. (11.24)
Neither in the oceans, nor in wells, nor in waterless pits, nor in lakes, nor in rivers, nor in streams, shall their movement ever be impeded. (11.25)

"If Śiva, the sustainer of the world, truly possesses the fivefold creative acts... (12.144)
By that truth, O nectar, O moon, O digit of the moon, flow forth!
If it be true that the goal of all scriptures is the vision of the Self. (12.145)
By that truth, let the nectar and the digits of the moon flow forth;
if it is true that Rati and Kāma have conquered the world through you.
By that truth, O nectar, moon, and digit of the moon, flow forth;
if it be true that Smara is the bestower of happiness upon all embodied beings.
By that truth, O nectar, O moon, O digit of the moon, flow forth! If it be true, O giver of supreme bliss, and if you be truly a noble donor! (12.148)
By that truth, O nectar, O moon, O digit of the moon, flow forth!
If this scripture is true, the supreme nectar of consciousness. By that truth, O nectar, O moon, O digit of the moon, flow forth!
If it be true that you, O Great Sovereign, are worthy of worship by all upon the lion-throne.
By that truth, O nectar, O moon, O essence of the crescent moon, flow forth;
for the command of the Guru is true, its manifestation unimpeded everywhere.
"By that truth, O nectar, flow forth as the moon's digit!
Immediately upon the recitation of these eight verses, she— || 12/152 ||
Even a messenger made of stone always runs away;
therefore, [he should be pursued] with that nectar which is pure, cool, and very light.

One should satisfy the fire of the *liṅga* with that which is the root of the power of irresistible will (*prākāmyasiddhi*), which bestows the speech of the *kaulinī*, and which has the very nature of the water of the Gaṅgā.

This is the full consecration (pūrṇābhiṣeka); this is the supreme final oblation (pūrṇāhuti). This is the limb of sacrificial offering; this is the path to absolute liberation (kaivalya). || 12.155 ||
This is the worship of Īśvara and this is the libation for Śakti;
this is the fruit of the knowledge of the Self, and this indeed is the fruit of the knowledge of the Self.
Since that Liṅga-Śaṅkara is worshipped with the eighth oblation, he,
being thus fully honored, bestows the state of Bhīma upon him.
The Lord of Khaṃsa makes everything—beginning with Bhīma—the locus of his own self;
he, together with his devotees, has attained purity through the nature of the supreme space. (12.158)
Extremely subtle, all-pervading, and entirely untainted,
he himself provides space for all beings, beginning with the earth.
One who is solely proficient in the bliss of the Self, whose nature is consciousness liberated from the objectified world,
is neither affected by merits nor by sins, nor by the various forms of virtue and vice.
Not by cold or heat, nor by pain or pleasure, nor by friends or enemies;
not by injuries or favors, nor by poverty or prosperity. (12.161)
Neither by hopelessness nor by craving, neither by defects nor by ornaments, nor by bondage or liberation is that which consists of the nectar of consciousness ever touched. (12.162)
O lady of beautiful hips, one perceives the entire universal wheel within one's own self;
therefore, one experiences it even as having the form of a city of Gandharvas.
One sees the God everywhere and sees everything within the God; what need is there for much speaking here? He is the direct bestower of bliss.
In this oblation, one should first use the mantras and the essences (rasas) born of the lunar digits;
thus has the consecration of the mantras for the second vessel been declared.
This eighth oblation itself is the female consort who gratifies Īśāna through her feminine form;
possessing the eightfold enjoyments, she bestows the status of sovereign over a great empire.
In this oblation, I shall describe the state of the messenger’s (dūtī) body:
the dissolution of consciousness in every aspect is the beauty of all her limbs. (12.167)
Her lotus-like eyes are half-closed due to the overflow of bliss; though they gaze in all directions, not even the slightest glance issues from their corners.
And in all his limbs there was the state of having sprouts of horripilation; yet there was no physical movement, no agitation, and no delirious moaning. (12.169)
There is no talk of intimacy, nor embracing, nor kissing; there is no biting with the teeth, nor seizing with a fist-blow, nor grasping by the hair. (12.170)
There were no dances of the hips, no tinkling of anklets, no jingling of the girdle, and no graceful movements of the limbs. (12.171)
The skill of weaving garlands of flowers does not delight him;
neither his falling down nor his rising up, nor the excellence of his physical means, [is pleasing].
Only the female messenger, casting aside the necklace of lotus-stalks placed upon her breast, [is seen].
The tremor produced in the region of the heart spreads to the very extremities.
Having understood such contempt for her, the unwise one would emit a drop during the great sacrifice of Ekāṣṭakā on the lunar fortnight. (12.174)
In the sequences beginning with the two aṣṭakas, there is no liberation from that in the middle;
therefore, beyond this, in the great sacrifice of the eight aṣṭakas, there is the group of eight dūtīs.
The vomiting of the Lord should be performed as an internal abundance of bliss;
for this indeed is the state of Śakti and Śambhu existing as one.
This is the supreme refuge for my devotees who possess such devotion;
thus, O Maheśvarī, has this Ānandayāga been described to you.
"He brings about all good fortune; what more do you wish to hear?
Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the Ānandatantra.
The Thirteenth Chapter.
109k) The Śrī Devī said:
O Lord, jewel of the crest of the Moon, by means of long-accumulated meritorious deeds, [I have attained this].
From the lotus of your mouth, Suśruta has heard the sequence of the eight oblations.
O God, no satiety arises for my ears from the pouring of this nectar;
O Lord of Gods, I desire to hear the sequence arising immediately after the sacrifice. (13.2)
"O Lord, tell me of the great significance of the sacrifice of passion (rati-yāga). O Goddess, O highly fortunate one, listen to that which you ask me, O Kāmeśvarī. (13.3)
By the mere realization of that, O Goddess, the hero becomes the omniscient Lord;
he is the Great Lord whose linga is weary from dancing for a very long time.
One should begin to describe the attainment of rest very gradually;
then, when the fall has been purified and filled with meritorious things.
One should satisfy the Īśāna-liṅga and the goddess Ānandabhairavī,
and recite the mantra of Ānandanātha twenty-eight times.
When the white and red [elements] have met within his own messenger (dūtī),
the wise one should hold them in the hollow of his right hand.
With the thumb and ring finger of his left hand, the practitioner, reciting the *kārikās*, should scatter drops from those two fingers which have been purified. (13.8)
May all the Bhairavas be satisfied; may Vaṭuka and the others be satisfied by these drops of white and red blood that delight the end of the sacrifice.
May the Blessed One Kāma be satisfied; may the goddesses of pleasure be satisfied. May he gladden the gods with these drops of white and red seed at the conclusion of the sacrifice.
May the goddesses of consciousness, who are established within my body, be satisfied by these drops of white and red [semen and blood] at the conclusion of the Ānandayāga. (13.11)
"May the circle of principles (tattvamandala), from Śiva down to the earthly element, be satisfied;
may they be gratified by these drops of white and red [semen and blood] until the end of the sacrifice."
May the Goddess Śrī, who bestows bliss and enjoyment, be forever satisfied everywhere by these drops of white and red [semen and blood] at the conclusion of the Ānandayāga.
O Goddess, may Consciousness and the Lord of Life, Śaṅkara, be forever satisfied by these drops of white and red [semen and blood] at the conclusion of the Ānandayāga.
May the supreme practitioners, whose heads are crowned by the feet of their own Lord, be satisfied by these drops of white and red [semen and blood] until the end of the Ānandayāga.
Reciting these eight verses for libation in this manner, the Lord of Lords (Nāthakendra) should satisfy the entire universe and his own self, O Great Goddess.
O Dear One, this very sacrifice is proclaimed as the "Great" (mahāyāga). Now, one should observe the messenger's (dūtī) desire, her gestures, and her sighing.
Her creeper-like limbs were thus loosened by the extreme force of enjoyment;
she was submerged in pure bliss and established in an inexpressible rasa.
She should cause her to attain a joy even greater than the experience of the bliss of Brahman;
she should awaken her gradually with cool, heart-pleasing, and gentle massages.
She should fan her with palm-leaf fans and wipe the perspiration from her face.
One should gladden the moon-like face with the gentle breeze of one's breath;
one should place substances possessing a refined fragrance into the mouth of the fire.
The root of the navel and the root of the thighs are as tender as young shoots.
One should massage her with one's own hand and snap the toes with the feet; by applying pressure with the hands to her shoulders, she will fall down. (13.22)
The wise man should massage the thighs and stroke the staff-like arms, especially around the house of passion (the genitals), with gentle hands. 13.23.
One should perform a massage and awaken her by means of that name: "Arise, arise, O auspicious one! This sacrifice has now fulfilled its purpose. (13.24)
O lady with thighs like the trunk of a plantain tree, I have been led by you to the ultimate pinnacle of bliss; for your limbs are as heart-delighting as the petals of the śirīṣa flower.
The commands of Śiva have now been transgressed by me, who am dependent on others;
forgive all of these, so that I may attain awakening once again. (13.26)
"O lady beautiful in all her limbs, this king of sacrifices has been completed by you;
therefore, arise and accept my great embrace"—thus he should awaken her. (13.27)
And by such flatteries as these, the family messenger was awakened; out of extreme joy, she manifested a state of helplessness through her very body. (13.28)
Slowly opening my eyes, which were clouded by the passion for worldly enjoyments, I have now experienced the very essence of supreme bliss. (13.29)
Oh, hero who goes before us! How marvelous is your skill!
Oh, what a great sacrifice for the propitiation of the Great Lord Liṅga!
112k) Oh, how great is the power of Ānandadeva’s vision!
Oh, I am satisfied, I am intoxicated; I have achieved my purpose to the highest degree. (13/31)
O Beloved, I, a wretched servant of Yours, shall perform service for You;
from birth until death, Your feet are my refuge.
If your favor toward me is such that a return for it is not possible, then at least accept me by embracing me to your own home. (13.33)
Having spoken thus, the Hero, embracing her who was agitated by the joy of his praise and embrace, should himself also embrace her and pass that night.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter in the Ānandatantra.
The Fourteenth Chapter.
Now, O Goddess of the Gods, I shall describe the majesty of the performance of the eight great sacrifices (mahāyāga), whose fruit is superior even to all other ritual offerings (kratu). 14.1.
The Great Sacrifice, the King of Sacrifices, the Sacrifice of Bliss, the Sacrifice of Delight, Liberation while Living, and the Great Oblation—thus is the Goddess. (14.2)
These are the successive stages of sacrifice: from the fruit of heaven comes liberation;
for those whose state is bound to the fruit, there arises the attainment of the station of the supreme Indra.
For those who sacrifice for the purpose of purifying the mind, liberation shall come to pass;
by means of this great sacrifice, O beautiful one, Indra attained his status as Indra.
The status of Viṣṇu belongs even to Viṣṇu, and likewise the nature of Brahman belongs to Brahmā;
the office of Rudra belongs to Rudra, and the lordship of the waters to Pracetas.
Other gods also possess such authority;
by this secret path, there shall be a battle against the difficult fortresses.
Therefore, this great sacrifice should be performed by those who desire happiness;
when being performed, it bears fruit, and once completed, it is the bestower of results. (14.7)
Even when merely heard, it cuts away evils root and branch;
even when spoken, it dispels [hostility] and binds one in friendship.
The fruits of his sacrificial rites, when performed, shall be offered to him;
there is no deed equal to this, and no austerity equal to this. (14.9)
There is no enjoyment equal to this, nor is there anything like it thereafter;
for this is the path upon which the way to liberation is easily traversed. (14.10)
By this, a person of good fortune attains [the goal] beyond measure;
this is an action more secret than the secret, indeed more hidden than the hidden. (14.11)

It must not be revealed to those who lack heroism, to those fallen from their lineage, to the sinful, to the evil-minded, to those of base conduct, or to those whose intellects are blinded by excessive anger. (14.12)
Toward those who are arrogant and heedless, who are full of sin, who are ignorant of what is beneficial and what is harmful, and who engage in futile quarrels— (14.13)
[One should not bestow it] upon those whose sole nature is jesting, those cursed by their gurus, lepers, fools who do not know the proper time, and those who oppose devotion to Hara. (14.14)

O Mother, [do not show such concern] for those who lack knowledge of others' minds, for the ill-favored, for the diseased, for those who have fallen from their high positions, for those who procrastinate, and for those who are virtuous. (14/15)
Among those who are stubborn, exceedingly greedy, attached to the wives of others, thieving, dull-witted, and nourishing themselves only with their bellies; || 14.16 ||
114k) Toward those who betray trust, toward betrayers of kinsmen, toward the arrogant, toward the contemptible, toward those of evil conduct, and toward powerful men who betray their strength; 14/17.

And toward those who are insane, toward rogues, toward those whose sole occupation is their tongues and genitals, toward those adhering to the doctrines of Cārvāka, and toward those who commit offenses against the gods; 14.18.
O Pārvatī, O auspicious lady, even among those who revile the illustrious Ānandadeva,
this great nectar of the King of Sacrifices is not to be disparaged.
The earth remains under the protection of Ānandanāthayājī;
that sacred land is proclaimed to extend for ten yojanas.
O Daughter of the Mountain, by him who has once in this life made this [lineage] full of blissful impressions, both families have been adorned by that very act.
His splendor increases, captivating even the great god of love; it is a moonlight that solidifies the ocean of joy in the eyes of women.
When the goddesses Vaśinī and the others constantly reside within her lotus-like mouth,
what need is there for the intense compositions of song by the female bees?
The protectors of the earth bow down, their crowns pressing against his feet,
considering themselves supremely fulfilled by the mere sight of him.
O Pārvatī, his power of command meets with no obstruction anywhere here on earth, just as the thunderbolt of Śakra meets no resistance upon the mountains.
All mantras, together with their presiding deities, come under his control;
he attains proficiency in the supernatural powers, beginning with *aṇimā*. (14.26)
At the mere sight of him, women melt like butter;
they follow even after fire, like dolls made of lac. (14.27)
Offering wealth, various objects, their own selves, and even their lives as gifts,
the wives of kings serve him.
Sins such as the killing of a Brahmin are destroyed by the mere sight of this [place].
Those who perform the supreme great sacrifice on these mountains [attain liberation]. (14.29)
Having gathered together with the sky-goers, they too become sky-goers—
those who perform the sacrifice in the middle of the forest at midnight.
By the very same method previously described, these beings also obtain strength;
having reached that place of strength amidst dwellings of blazing jewels.
In the world of the nāgas, the nāga maidens enjoy and partake of pleasures;
therefore, this great sacrifice is difficult to obtain even for the gods.
Having learned from the scripture or from the mouth of the guru, one who practices becomes victorious;
otherwise, O Goddess, ruin arises from practicing incorrectly. (14.33)
This sacrifice has faith as its root; faith is the life of sacrifice.
O lady of beautiful hips, one lives by placing trust in this authoritative path.
In this world, there has never been, nor will there ever be, anything equal to trust—whether in performing mantras, in administering medicine, or in relation to a deity or a guru. (14.35)
One who maintains faith indeed attains the fruit as described;
whereas through lack of faith, doubt, and the delusions of futile reasoning, one reaps nothing.
Due to performing [rites] without faith, the lowest of men surely falls;
behold the greatness of faith in stone, wood, clay, and so forth. (14.37)
116k) Since it is through his grace that he bestows dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, by what means could an insentient, inert substance grant spiritual accomplishment? (14.38)
In that regard, the root must be sought; therein, trust is the cause.
Both ritual action and faith, as well as the tradition, are the two factors that set it in motion.
Faith, when nurtured by these two, bestows perfection;
for even those of the lowest castes, such as Caṇḍālas and others, who are always impure and foolish, [attain it]. (14.40)
If there is no faith in the mantras that destroy poison, they do not yield their fruit;
nor is there proper conduct, nor purity, nor scholarship, nor the qualities of intellect. (14.41)
The cause of the attainments of mantras is faith; therein, faith is the cause. Faith is defined as the firmness of the mind in the practice of mantra-sādhana.
"In every way, may the accomplishment of my desired object occur here"—thus having gained confidence, he who seeks the fruit becomes the very embodiment of that fruit. (14.43)
By means of this scripture, a learned person who wanders about shall attain the state of a praiser of Him;
herein, the authority for instruction belongs to the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas. (14.44)
For those of the Śūdra or lower castes, the supreme duty is the service of them;
for them, the fulfillment of their desired fruits lies in the service of the Vīras. (14.45)
The duty of a Brahmin should always be performed; that of a Kṣatriya, at the front of battle; that of a Vaiśya, for the sake of profit from trade; but never that of a Śūdra or others. (14.46)
Mudrās, however, should always be accepted; there is no restriction regarding them based on caste.
Only that single caste known as "woman" should be accepted, provided the requisite characteristics are present. (14.47)

117k) When endowed with the characteristics of a messenger (*dūtī*), women of all kinds are to be accepted; for these deer-eyed ones were created by me as the means for worship and accomplishment. (14/48)
He who possesses a bamboo flute (vaṃśa) is here devoid of blemish; however, cows are pure at their backs, while those who speak are pure in their mouths.
The Brahmin is pure from his feet upward; women are pure in every part.
The mouth of a woman is always pure; no impurity from food remains there. (14.50)
They must always be worshipped by those who abide by all the established doctrines;
for without them, there is no sacrifice, no austerity, and no vow.
Neither worship nor supreme sovereignty, nor even the sacrifice of bliss, is the primary element;
rather, the messenger-women (dūtī) are declared to be the principal factor in the great sacrifice of the eight oblations.
Having brought the Heroic Fortune (vīralakṣmī) as the heroine to this leader of the seat (pīṭha), she joins them together; therefore, she is proclaimed as the messenger (dūtī). (14.53)
The word *dū* signifies evil, and the word *tri* signifies its cessation;
therefore, the wise have called *dūtī* that which removes anxiety and distress. (14.54)
O Maheśvarī, Dūtikā, Kulaśakti, Pūjāpūrti, and Bhoginībhogalakṣmī are the synonymous epithets for her. (14.55)
A female messenger who is disciplined, sweet-spoken, and endowed with beauty cannot be obtained by all people without having performed difficult austerities. (14.56)
Therefore, one should not harbor hatred toward those female messengers;
one should not proclaim their faults, nor should one behave unkindly toward them. (14.57)
One should not touch their vital points with words spoken by those who pierce the vital points;
rather, having seen any woman whatsoever, one should contemplate her as a deity.
One should always behave in this manner toward those female messengers (dūtīs) who are worthy of worship;
otherwise, one may act according to one's desire, yet one should treat them with gentleness.
Gentleness toward all women bestows merit and happiness; Ātreya [Kh: -bhojana-] [bestows] it through the eating of old food, and Kapila [bestows] it through compassion for living beings. (14.60)
O Pāñcālī, one should place Bṛhaspati in the absence of trust, Triṣu in mildness, and Ārdrā near the time of sacrifice, even when there is a separation from the proper timing. (14.61)
Beholding her face in this manner, one should mutter the mantra of Ānanda;
for if one should mutter it without her, who is intoxicated by the god of love, [the practice is fruitless].
Like moonlight in a forest, that knowledge of his would be fruitless;
therefore, this greatness of the Mahāyāga has been proclaimed.
Furthermore, O auspicious one of beautiful hips, what do you desire to hear?
[Thus ends] the fifteenth chapter.
The Goddess said:
O God of gods, I have heard the entire definition of the Great Sacrifice (mahāyāga) and its majesty as proclaimed by you; it is an elixir for the ears of those who hear.
This sacrifice has the female messenger as its primary element; it is for the purpose of pleasing the messenger.
O Great Lord, what is the means? For they, when impassioned, are indeed the bestowers of accomplishment. (15.2)
Those who are not attached do not bestow happiness, nor do those who are detached bring about prosperity; it is with these women who are devoted that one's purpose in action is accomplished. (15.3)

By what means can there be any pleasing of them? For by their very nature they are fickle; seized by many faults like those possessed by evil planets, their hearts are corrupted by crookedness. (15.4)
O Lord, those women who are always known as "left-handed" (vāmā) because of their crooked nature—
tell me the means for this, for this is what I wish to hear.
"O sweet-voiced one, mistress of desire, I shall tell you all of that; let it be understood:
women are fickle by nature and possess many faults. (15.6)
O Mother, no cause whatsoever is considered to exist for their coloring [of their feelings];
for there is no trust in a woman that "she is devoted to me.
Indeed, genuine, unartificial affection is very difficult to find among women in all circumstances.
With a certain expression on his face, his eyes slightly narrowed. || 15/8 ||
How can there be trust in the playful conversations of women? They possess many arts of illusion and are greedy for many lovers. (15.9)
The deer-eyed women of the low-born, possessing various dispositions, forcibly captivate the mind with their many enchanting charms. (15.10)
Having rendered the person powerless, it does not destroy his attachment;
for the person who is of a single nature, it is like a pure crystal. (15.11)
In this world, women possess deceitful conduct and no genuine intention;
those who are actually attached appear as if detached, while those who are detached appear as if full of longing. (15.12)
The inner essence of women is not understood by anyone—
not by those with claws, nor by rivers, nor by horned creatures, nor by those who carry weapons in their hands. (15.13)
In the case of women and kings, trust is the root-cutter;
though they are filled with affection by their husbands through various kinds of prostrations at every moment. (15.14)
Even sisters-in-law must necessarily have different minds;
this cannot be overcome by enjoyment, nor by wealth, nor by the offering of non-opposition. (15.15)
Neither by weapons nor by treatises can those three types of crooked people be subdued in any way;
they are tormented by the suffering of sweat, yet they find constant pleasure in it.
In whose family is there no fault? Under whose control are women with eyes like those of a doe? Even in a forest devoid of men, they have been stationed for a hundred autumns.
Having mentally created a person, they enjoy the cessation found therein;
by whom has the face of sciences—not like that of women—not been kissed with the lips? 15.18
There are few men who capture the hearts of women;
yet, embracing their husbands with vine-like arms whose bracelets jingle, they remain so. (15.19)
Wandering women bestow their hips upon another man, even upon a paramour;
not by Brahmā, nor by Śakra, nor by me, nor by Viṣṇu can they be restrained.
It is not at all possible to discern their true nature within themselves, even if they are guarded at every moment by hundreds of walls. (15.21)
Women, intoxicated by passion, delight other men;
they are capable of corrupting women and even deluding others. (15.22)
The capacity inherent in their very origin does not depend on training;
for no one can grasp the minds of those women, owing to their extreme restlessness. (15.23)

O Pārvatī, the wind should be restrained by means of the *gṛdhra* (vulture) posture; likewise, the waves are suppressed by the *ekapāda* (one-footed) posture, as well as by the *gajakarṇa* (elephant-ear), *taṭit-dhāman* (lightning-splendor), and *cala-patra* (moving-leaf) postures. 15/24.
The minds of women are by their very nature exceedingly fickle;
there is never any satisfaction of the mind, nor is there ever satiety in any activity whatsoever. (15.25)
Not even by ten million men could the deer-eyed women be satisfied in their enjoyment;
they thought of one another, their actions concealing their inner intentions.
Women delude men with artificial passion;
yet they feel no mental distress even through life-threatening acts of recklessness. (15.27)
And neither does one who fears sin feel fear, nor is there reverence for the teachings;
fire is never satiated with wood, nor is the great ocean by rivers. (15.28)
Among all beings here, there are no eunuchs with beautiful eyes;
for women, food is double and the intellect is fourfold.
Sāhasa is said to have six qualities, and Kāma is considered to be eightfold;
thus, in connection with the Mahāyāga, the eightfold Kāma has been proclaimed by me. (15.30)

By means of the flow that opens the mouth of the channels (nāḍīs) such as Candronmattā and others, there arises [the sight] of those women with eyes like lotus petals and eyebrows like the feathers of a swan. 15.31.
For what reason would the minds of women not be crooked? If their minds were ever to become attached to a man anywhere, [they would surely be straight]. (15.32)
Then there is no talk of enjoyment from his mouth, nor does pleasure arise;
the water of enjoyment does not flow forth, nor do the riches of delusion exist. (15.33)
Happiness does not arise for men when the hearts of women are set elsewhere;
therefore, I shall describe the supreme mind of those with eyes like a deer's as it moves toward another. (15.34)
One should protect one's wife by means of various graceful gestures, as well as through the wealth of beauty, charm, speech, pleasure, and erotic sentiment. (15.35)
The longing for another man arises in women quite fruitlessly, occurring solely through the power of delusion. (15.36)
Concealing themselves, they delight even the wise with their gestures; yet the foolish and the stubborn do not recognize the underlying intention behind such artificial behavior.
Thinking, "She is devoted to me," they strive for pleasure in vain;
alas, the physical gestures and conduct of women are difficult to discern by a fool! (15.38)
Only the clever understand the distinction between artificial and natural conduct; indeed, it is the fair-eyed women who are the deceivers of all deceivers.

Even such women as these deceive men who are full of pride; though they are experts in the scriptures, the lecherous ones delude even those who understand the scriptures through their own teachings. (15.40)
Even one who is the best among those skilled in statecraft, even one who possesses far-sighted vision, even one who wields the rope as a weapon, and even one who is expert in protection— (15.41)
Even one possessed of pride, even one exalted by energy,
even one who is haughty, even one who is angry, even a thief, and even a lord— [15.42]
Moreover, he stands at the forefront of mature combat, acting as a snake-charmer in capturing the serpents of the hearts of women. (15.43)
O Maheśvarī, the winning over of the minds of those female messengers occurs through excellent conduct, just as it does for a hero. (15.44)
The conduct regarding the female messengers (dūtīs) is revealed here in detail;
the hero should employ them for the purpose of achieving passion. (15.45)
In the Ārata-tantra, their conduct is regulated in many ways;
the minds of these women find no other refuge than the preceptors. (15.46)
Supreme gentleness is their means of winning affection;
likewise, patience toward lapses and the careful examination of faults. (15.47)
One should never strike them, nor speak harshly, nor harbor malice toward women;
indeed, the rod of punishment ought not to be applied to women. (15.48)
If, O Goddess, they disregard even the loss of their lives like blades of grass, behold the audacity of these women now that their own husband has gone to heaven. (15.49)
To women whose husbands are like blazing fires, a forest of red lotuses becomes a place of torment; through the harshness of perspiration and beatings, they seem to surrender their very lives.
But deer-eyed women do not take as their object the mere movement of living beings;

128k) The Śrī Devī said:
O God of gods, you who are marked with the trident and who bestow joy upon the world!
The established order for all women and the established order for men. || 16/1 ||
O Lord, tell me of that which has been conceptualized according to the very path taught in the scriptures;
eighty-four hundred thousand species are proclaimed to exist.
O Śaṅkara, among all those women, no fixed distinction exists such that "this woman's husband is this man" and "that woman's husband is that man. (16.3)
Those dharmas which were previously established by the one who devised the boundaries, on account of the equality of their genus, are the dharmas among the human species. (16.4)

O Lord, what more can be said? This establishment of merit and sin, this regulation of dharma and adharma, and the ostentation of the Vedas, scriptures, and so forth—[all these are but a fabrication]. (16.5)
O Treasure of Wisdom, having ascertained the reason for this, please tell me: for what purpose were the specific modes of conduct established for the human race? (16.6)
"O Goddess, you have spoken the truth: Kāmeśvara is equal to all the classes of gods."
For all classes of beings, there are eating, drinking, and deep sleep.
There is nothing else superior to this, nor is there anything more abundant for a human being;
O Goddess, this is the cause, and it is declared therein to be the cause.
O beloved, an undertaking without a cause never occurs anywhere;
those who know the tantra of the means to achieve desired ends do not exist in all births.

Even for deer and other such creatures, this awareness consists merely in the appeasement of hunger by eating grass; and for all birds as well, it is simply the nourishing of their young with their own food. (16.10)
Even for cows and the like, you maintain that there is a defect toward a man holding grass in his hand;
yet, upon seeing one with a staff in his hand, they act falsely out of fear. (16/11)
Nourished by love for his own calf, he meditated on that calf as longing for milk; yet, even through meditation on the calf's mother, he found no peace. (16.12)
Some say that cattle and other such beings are insentient because they lack consciousness;
O Daughter of the Mountain, how can there be a lack of consciousness? (16.13)
The cognition that something is a means to achieve a desired end is present everywhere;
indeed, the understanding of even animals is observed to be like that of humans. (16.14)
Moreover, compared to us humans, animals possess great agility;
for instance, they build their nests with blades of grass held firmly in their beaks. (16.15)
That nest was exceedingly dense, wonderfully variegated,
possessing a concealed interior, and free from the afflictions of rain and wind.
Behold this marvel: having placed mud upon its beak, it is devoured there at the edge of the mud by a firefly shining in the night.
When the nest-house is illuminated by that lamp made of [the essence of] him, the bird enters it together with his mate, surely enjoying [it]. 16.18.
Behold the cocoon spun by the silkworm;
its expansion and its contraction—that is knowledge, not arrogance. (16.19)
O lady of beautiful hips, another, having seized a worm and leading it to the state of its own self as a bee, demonstrates that proficiency in one's own species has been attained.
130k) O Daughter of the Mountain, behold the cleverness of the *vajrakīṭa* insect as it fashions wheels of uniform shape upon the *śāligrāma* stones. (16.21)
"O beautiful one, behold the swan's discrimination between water and milk;
even by Brahmā, such a course of action could not be accomplished. (16.22)
O lady of beautiful hips, even when all directions are enveloped in dense darkness during the night, the owl perceives jars and other objects. (16.23)
O lady of excellent complexion, among all those castes, the ritual procedure proceeds with greater intensity toward a higher caste, and it is impossible for one caste to affect another. (16.24)
How could such a person, being a fool like a beast, describe Buddhahood? His doctrine is merely empty, inflated vanity. (16.25)
But there are four things common to all embodied beings, O beloved:

Therefore, what is this arrogant and stubborn insistence of fools?

The wise know that at each successive age, there is a further decline in the conduct of mortal beings;

In the Tretā age, O Maheśvarī, Dharma has three feet and possesses measure; in the Dvāpara, it consists of the form of Artha, and in the Kali age, it is characterized by the conduct of the learned.
By means of these four ages, the fluctuations of the minds— possessing diverse modes of activity—
arise, dissolve, and expand again and again.
And at times the activities of mortal beings contract, just as men abide in righteousness during the periods of the Kṛta and other ages. (16.31)
At that time, there was no desire to cause harm, nor fickleness, nor manliness;

Because everyone has accomplished their task, there is nothing further to be done;

Then, O Goddess, that which consists of mantra is always perceived;

That alone belongs to these men, and not even crooked conduct;

Again, by the power of time, within that human race,

Endowed with the four states arising from that, consciousness thus awakens:

May all objects of enjoyment belong to me alone;

"But I am powerful, mature, skillful, and possess many means; having slain this weakling, I shall enjoy captivating pleasures. (16.52)
Thus, through passion for objects of enjoyment and through envy toward those associated with them, they engage in mutual strife by means of mutual destruction. (16.53)
