For one thing appears in a certain way through the intellect, yet it does not appear that way for another;
indeed, due to the diversity of inclinations here, there are many millions of scriptures.
The form of all things here is conceived as twofold:
the science of polity (arthaśāstra) and, O lady of beautiful hips, from those two arises the emergence of the treatise (śāstra).

In every scripture, the established doctrines, logical arguments, and reasons, as well as the means of valid cognition such as direct perception and the rest—this alone is the cause in every respect. (17.19)
O Goddess, although there is a multiplicity of means of valid cognition, for some there is brevity, for others equality; thus, this process of valid knowledge is threefold.

"O lady of beautiful hips, who among the Lokāyatikas has declared that perception alone is the [means of knowledge]? Both the followers of the Sugata and the followers of Kaṇāda have taught perception and inference. (17.21)
The Sāṃkhyas declared that there are three means of valid cognition—perception, inference, and verbal testimony;
others who belong to a single school of Nyāya are likewise proclaimed to hold the same view as the Sāṃkhyas.

Some maintain that there are perception, inference, and verbal testimony; others have declared that these four, together with presumptive testimony (arthāpatti), constitute the means of knowledge. (17.23)
Another seeks five types of pride together with non-existence;
some here [assert] that it arises through these six types of pride when combined.
Led by those well-versed in the Purāṇas, they carry out their legal proceedings;
herein, the learned disputants include one another within their respective arguments. (17.25)
Conceiving themselves to be arbiters, the arrogant ones quarreled among themselves:
"Whose possession is greater, and whose possession is smaller? (17.26)
Of these two, the former falters due to the weight of that which must be protected;
those who, being conceited, make only a slight study of the scriptures. (17.27)
Those Buddhists and others, heroes of logic, shake their opponents;
and shaking their doctrines with the brilliant knots of reasoning, they prevail. (17.28)
Others maintain that their own established doctrines are fixed;
such being the case, there would be conflict and disorder among all the scriptures. (17.29)
Among speakers, [the distinction between] the literal and the figurative arises only through these two;
some who speak according to their own natural inclination reject that which is born of figurative attribution. (17.30)
And its preventers are others that establish superimposition;
O Daughter of the Mountain, I shall now describe the nature of superimposition. (17.31)
Or rather, because it is rooted in verbal designation (*śabda*), superimposition (*āropa*) consists of mere words;
for this entire earth, though appearing in various forms, is indeed nothing but clay. (17.32)
Wherein abundant forms are produced by the thousands—this earth is merely clay, kneaded by the hands of the potter. (17.33)

O Daughter of the Mountain, when that very same lump of clay has acquired another name, "clod of earth," it is then, by means of the potter’s manual operations upon that lump of clay, [transformed]. (17.34)
In the Middle Country, which was made profound by the clear evidence of the activities of the staff, the robes, the wheel, and so forth, it was there that [the doctrine] was hollowed out. (17.35)
And with its front [part] having its opening closed, standing with a neck like a conch shell, it partakes in being the denotation of the word "pitcher" (kuṃbha). (17.36)
Furthermore, O lady of beautiful hips, that very same body, crushed by the blow of the staff,
with all its limbs shattered upon the ground, seeks to become a mass of skulls.
But when that very lump of clay is pounded by the striking of hammers, pestles, and the like, being thus crushed, it attains the state of being denoted by the word "dust. (17.38)
That very same thing, O fortunate one, when tossed by the fierce and impetuous wind,
becomes shattered again and again, and through its force once more desires the state of being a particle of dust in the sky.
And among those *trasareṇu*s,
those which have resorted to heaviness fall to the great earth and once again assume the state of dust;
whereas those very same *trasareṇu*s that have attained extreme lightness remain here as they are.
Extremely subtle and difficult to perceive, it whirls within the sphere of wind.
Thus, many transformations of the lump of clay itself remain; these are proclaimed as superimpositions (āropas) that cannot be described by one another's names. (17.42)
O Beloved, while some desire this and others accomplish it, the wise man effects the imposition of form upon the jar and other objects therein. (17.43)
How can its reality be denied by another who asserts its truth, merely because of the association with other qualities, as in the case of clay? (17.44)
Why would one superimpose some other property such as "jar-ness" and speak of it?
Its superimposition is in vain, and its subsequent dissolution is likewise in vain. (17.45)
The attribution of the status of "Veda" is refuted by adversaries;
such indeed are the causes established for this quarrel. (17.46)
Moreover, even elsewhere, such a movement [of meaning] occurs from a word like "biṃboṣṭhī" (the bimba-lipped one);
however, as for those words that consist of phonemes (varṇas), their individual permanence [is maintained]. (17.47)
The opponent asserts impermanence regarding both [the self and the aggregates]; even there, logical arguments [are applicable].
Therefore, for those disputants whose enmity has increased and who are leaping forward [in debate], [this is the case]. (17.48)

For those whose intellects are clouded by the obsession with their own scholarship and who are blinded by excessive pride, seeking the logic that establishes the objects they themselves have embraced, [this work is intended]. (17.49)
For those who have accepted their own view and seek out the flaws in the opposing view, by means of that search and with a concentration equal to it, [the opponent's position is undermined]. (17.50)

146k) For those who act in contradiction [to their own tenets] by exposing the flaws in their own treatises, or who speak in contradiction [to logic], one should employ the points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) such as the fallacies of genus (*jāti*). (17.51)
There is the loss of one's thesis and the infliction of suffering by those who are preeminent; when anger arises later, there is the shouting of cries that cause the throat to wither. || 17.52 ||
With great egotism, let them engage in hand-to-hand combat;
again, in that manner, let the battle proceed with hair-pulling.

When that which produces agitation has arisen, through the awakening of further reflection, the force of those disputants—who are like those whose momentum has been checked—is brought to rest from its very foundation within the abodes of hatred. (17.54)

[This is established] by those who remain in a state of non-delusion through their actions, who do not perceive [duality], who lack [subjective] realization, who have formulated their own tenets, whose minds are purified, and who are censured by others. (17.55)
This is their unrestrained path, belonging to those who, by means of various other doctrines, cause people to become utterly deluded regarding the sequence that is identical to their own. (17.56)
The sixteen categories accepted by Gautama as the constituent parts of inference, which are rooted in the means of valid cognition—by means of these, the great Kali [is propitiated]. (17.57)
O lady of beautiful hips, no established doctrine arises from mere debate;
therein there is only quarreling, brought about by hundreds of ill-spoken arrows. (17.58)
Through the destruction of birth, restraint, and killing, there occurs the complete exhaustion of the foot;
at that time, the determination will be made by the left side, taking the form of attainment.
That is not possible, for even when the definition of genus and so forth is to be examined and has been reached, it is only debate that proceeds. (17.60)
By what means would there be the attainment of that debate?
For it is through the application of *jāti* (futile rejoinders) and *nigraha* (points of defeat) that the conclusion of the debate is achieved and the establishment of victory is attained. (17.61)
But if the victory in the debate is established by the suppression of the [opponent's] position, then the demonstration of that debate is through the fault of mutual dependence. (17.62)
But treatises of this kind, which rely solely on the power of inducing sleep, are mutually contradictory and do not produce wonder. (17.63)
By mutually obstructing one another through the distinction between the sublated and the sublator, the various misconceptions appear as mutual invalidity. (17.64)
Therefore, all these [scriptures] are deviations from that respective path;
another person there does not perceive their authority. || 17.65 ||
In that situation, the radiance of the gaze of the neutral observer serves as the form of the proximate object for both the disputants and their adversaries who are possessed of great pride.

The mediator is one who stands between the two opposing sides, discerning merits and defects, and who understands the truth of the skillful reasoning presented by both the proponent and the opponent. (17.67)
"Practicing all things with a clear intellect," he thus declares:
"Come, all you proponents and their opponents! (17.68)
Establishment and refutation are equal by way of reasoning; likewise, fault and virtue are equal, and even the low and the high are considered equal. (17.69)
When a fault is equal for both sides and the rebuttal is likewise equal, one should not be singled out for censure in such an investigation of the matter. (17.70)
In a system where everyone is equal, there should be no proclamation of faults against any single individual.
Therefore, for those who prioritize equality, it is not appropriate to harbor hatred toward anyone other than [those who violate that principle]. (17.71)
Listen to the nature of the equality of the Pradhāna; I shall explain it:
whatever action there may be, and whichever deity there may be—whatever it may be. (17.72)
Whatever the object of worship may be in the ritual of worship, and whoever the worshipper may be, whatever liberation is described in every scripture is said to be the same. (17.73)
Therefore, it was Kali who brought about this state of manifoldness for you, as you encountered the various divisions of the collection of ritual acts and so forth. (17.74)
Having indeed discharged that debt through your own successive stages of rice cultivation, O Ānanda, for me, Maheśvara, who am situated in the midst of those such as you; ||| 10 ||
For one who serves the established conclusion, which consists of bliss and is the very form of knowledge, knowledge characterized by bliss is found even in all the scriptures. (17.76)
Indeed, when form is set aside, what is it that has entered into your thoughts? Upon investigation, even its very existence as a basis for all conventional usage ceases to be.
The wise perceive nothing other than the Supreme, whose body is knowledge and bliss;
that [Supreme] is knowledge, its nature is bliss, it is all-pervading, and it is the source of all births.
The wise serve Him whose form is indivisible and who dwells within the darkness;
thus, for the Great Lord who is the bliss of one's own self, He exists in a form that is intermediate.
Thus, when the defects of their minds have been cleansed by the nectar of reasoned speech, the wise accept it as "so it is," in accordance with both their own and new scriptures. (17.80)
From that time forth, O lady of beautiful limbs, even the various scriptures have indeed come to be regarded as mere limbs in the presence of the vision of great bliss. (17.81)

Therefore, starting from the square of the outer enclosure of the Śrī Lalitā-cakra, one should worship, in due order, one's own scriptures such as the Cārvāka and others, beginning with the entry. || 17.82 ||
Whichever [constellations] are situated on the outside are indeed weak; whichever are situated on the inside are indeed very powerful.
Now, for this great scripture, which is a vast ocean of various paths, there are retinues and guardians, as well as collections of treatises intended for its protection. (17.84)

Arising from the play of one's own respective consciousness, those who have blocked the emergence of the dākinīs and others certainly become the path of the scriptures and serve as limbs of the Vīra-mārga.
Moreover, their status as auxiliary limbs consists in being causes for the human goal;
however, the primary human goal is that which brings about the great sacrifice.
O lady with eyes like those of the *cakora* bird, some say that wealth is the form of reality that sets worldly activity in motion;
others say it is the goal of human endeavor, leading to virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation.
That opinion is not captivating to the mind, for virtue and liberation consist in the state of being free.
For the yoga of bliss is, above all, the means for accomplishing that.
Therefore, there is neither the person nor the purpose of the person;
indeed, Dharma alone is the great sacrifice that bestows both seen and unseen fruits. (17.89)
That very same desire is also liberation, because it consists of the bliss of enjoyment; that very same thing is also liberation in Śiva, because it consists of supreme bliss.
150k) By the Vedic declarations remembered as "Ānanda is the form of Brahman," the Puruṣa is the embodiment of Dharma, the embodiment of Desire, and the embodiment of Liberation. || 17/91 ||
Half of that human purpose is declared to be of the nature of wealth;
for wealth is indeed the primary means for the worship of Maheśa.

Neither perfumes, flowers, incense, and the like, nor anything lacking in fragrance, can come into being; neither an object of extreme fragrance, nor an exceedingly fine cloth [can exist without them]. (17.93)
O Goddess of the Gods, there were no ornaments that brought joy, nor were there any pleasant fruits, nor any ripe fruits. (17.94)
Neither the goal nor the means of attainment appear, nor is there even a pleasant thought;
without wealth, the aims of human life do not succeed—this is what has been declared. (17.95)
Therefore, he who was previously described as the preeminent among speakers is indeed the Lord;
yet he did not abandon all the scriptures, even though they were devoid of meaning.
That Ānandamaheśāna ordained that the study of sciences such as logic (tarka) and others is the primary cause for bestowing wealth upon embodied beings.
Only for one of human birth is there a need for wealth and possessions;
not for a being belonging to another species, because such things are easily obtained [or, because they are naturally provided]. (17.98)
As soon as it arises, for the most part, other birth nourishes itself;
but this human birth, by means of these purifications, nourishes the self.
Thus, for those born as humans, the meeting and gathering together has been accomplished;
yet it is difficult indeed to seek one another out. (17.100)
O Goddess, the desire for wealth through the path of seeking it is extremely painful and is the sole vessel for manifold sufferings. (17.101)
Therefore, Maheśvara exists for the sake of providing food for men, for the heroes to perform worship of their own selves, and for the acquisition of wealth. || 17/102 ||
And all the scriptures, though fruitless, were preserved even then for the sake of deluding others, O Daughter of the Mountain. (17.103)
Speaking in the manner that will be described, they wander about, exclaiming:
"Aho! I know the Sāṃkhya scripture; I know the sacrificial altar; I know the water-offering. I am consecrated; I possess good karma; I am eternally one who maintains the Agnihotra fire."
"I am a master of mantras, I am a perfected one (siddha), I am a scholar, and I am a poet.
I am a knower of logic and scripture; I am proficient in Mīmāṃsā.
I am a knower of the true meaning of the Vedas, and I am capable in the science of sacrifice."
I am the knower of the Smṛtis, the sacrifices, and the Jyotiṣāmayaṇa; indeed, I alone on this earth am the knower of the truth of the Vedas and their six auxiliary limbs.
"I am of noble birth; my kinsmen are wise men. I have taken a wife from a pure Brahmin family; indeed, I am a master of eloquence. (17.108)
I am the one to be known; I am capable of performing every act of expiation;
I am ignorant of the flavors of food today; yet I am proficient in poetic discourse. (17.109)
"I am a master of the Vedānta, composing great literary works"—with such words, arrogant with pride and mixed with both truth and falsehood, [he spoke]. (17.110)
They delude foolish kings who have fallen from the path of what is beneficial and harmful; blinded by the pride of delusion, the wealthy worship them with those very riches.
Then, having obtained those riches bestowed through their learning, the fools accumulate them solely for the purpose of satisfying their own appetites. (17.112)
Those wise ones who know Ānandadeva to be the Lord (Īśāna) are established in their respective scriptures and strive for wealth for the purpose of worship. (17.113)
O beautiful one, O lady of lovely limbs, these scriptures are for the purpose of deluding the wealthy and for the sake of concealing the truth, not for the realization of reality.
O Daughter of the Mountain, the path to the realization of reality exists only in this Ānandatantra; it is not found anywhere else.
"Truth, truth, and again truth—raising up my arm, I declare this:
O fair-browed one, this which has become reality is called the Great Sacrifice. (17.116)
The nature of the Great Sacrifice (mahāyāga) has been set forth in this tantra;
now the principles and the established tenets of this tantra are being demonstrated.
There is no destruction of anything whatsoever, nor is there a transition into another quality; rather, manifestation and disappearance occur in all things. (17.118)
Wise men cannot say that there is either origination or destruction based on this alone;
it is not as if Devadatta, upon leaving his house, has lost his prior identity. (17.119)
Indeed, it is only by means of the word "arisen" that one can engage in conventional usage; Devadatta is not [perceived] when he is concealed by his entering [the house] from his coming out. (17.120)
Even the state of being denotable by the word "destroyed" is perceived [in that case].
Likewise, when Devadatta is born from his mother's womb, even the slightest suspicion of his [re-]origination does not warrant being connected there. (17.121)
Without manifestation, no other kind of origination is possible.
If it is maintained that "being produced" consists in being something other than manifestation, then upon investigation, that [position] does not prove attractive at all. (17.123)

For it has been demonstrated right at the beginning that neither by mere association nor by being included among the qualities does there exist a state of being produced or a state of being qualified. (17.124)
Time, space, and the sky likewise have sound alone as their singular form; yet they possess no ultimate reality, being born solely from conventional usage.
When time is investigated, only action remains;
when the directions are investigated, only space; and when the sky is investigated, only the wind. (17.126)
Therefore, O daughter of the mountain, these—earth, water, fire, air, sound, darkness, and mind—are merely residual designations for sound (śabda). (17.127)
O Supreme Goddess, the categories of existence are declared to be "the individual soul" (jīva) and "Śiva"; it is through this very duality that all categories of existence manifest. (17.128)
These nine remain; these are the many forms of the One.
The collective, the individual, the ritual action, and so forth—there is no counting of them. (17.129)
The duality there is without support; in each case, it rests upon the sevenfold sequence.
Like wind or a visual impairment, the Arhat has no accumulation whatsoever anywhere.
O Goddess, the remaining others also abide within their own substrates;
these nine substances have been proclaimed in the Great Scripture (Mahāgama). 17/131.
Forms are entirely devoid of sound and other qualities;
having established a manifold number of these very forms through their various distinctions. (17.132)
The principles are established differently in each respective treatise;
O Pārvatī, direct perceptual experience is found in all of these.
Earth, water, fire, darkness, and the eye are within the range of direct perception.
When there is water or darkness, [the color] is white; when there is wind, it is pure earth; and its form is variegated.
O Daughter of the Mountain, fire possesses all colors and, it is said, has an additional quality of luminosity; wind, however, has touch as its object of perception.
Sound, which is to be grasped by auditory perception, resides in the one who speaks like a cuckoo;
all things are subject to the mind and life-force, and they themselves are the means of valid cognition.

The means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) are said to be threefold, consisting of verbal testimony (śabda), the senses (akṣa), and inference (anumā). Among these, verbal testimony consists of the speech of authoritative persons (āpta), as well as the Vedas, sciences, and scriptures. (17.137)
Direct perception (*adhyakṣa*) is divided into two types: that which has one part perceived and that which has one part unperceived.
That which is perceived is indeed direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), while the second is known as inference (*anumā*).
In reality, there is no conceptualization of a difference between inference and perception;
for when the qualified part is seen, there is the perception of that which possesses it. (17.139)

If this were so, then there would be no possibility of cutting a jar or similar objects by means of perception; for if it is argued that the jar remains perceptible because its entire nature has been seen, [then the following applies]. (17.140)

155k) However, because the rays of the eye do not reach the far side of the jar, the entire form of the jar is not perceived; thus, the cognition of the jar does not occur with respect to the jar [itself]. (17.141)
Therefore, no real distinction between these two has been proclaimed;
for both are the crowning jewels of the collection of means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), being designated by the term "perception" (adhyakṣa).
O lady with tremulous eyes, it is accepted in the Vihānanda-tantra that even in worldly transaction, the requirement of a triad is here considered necessary.
Therefore, O Maheśvarī, these eight have been declared to be perceivable by direct perception;
now, the ninth, the Śiva-tattva, is to be understood here through verbal testimony.
But when this Lord of Life is perfected through the Great Sacrifice, having abandoned the state of being manifested by words, he shines forth by his own direct perception. (17.145)
The establishment of reality has been declared; now hear about the supported and the support:
wind is the support of one [element], while darkness is remembered as being indifferent. (17.146)
The group of seven, excluding Śiva, is held to have the Maruts as its support;
Śiva, however, is the support of all—this is correctly analyzed therein.
Just as the wind-circle [is in] the wind, and water [is] in the earth; and in the earth, through forms such as the Siddhas and others, there exists the nature of wind, cloud, and snow. (17.148)
Fire should be known as residing within me; fire is that which burns and provides warmth.
O beloved, it is said that sound resides in earth, water, and wind. (17.149)
O Goddess, the mind and the life-force—these two are the glorious aggregates;
and the aggregate of earth and the other elements is proclaimed as the body. (17.150)
Therefore, O Goddess, having determined that which is manifold and endowed with consciousness, that which is impelled by the vital breath (prāṇa) is here called "sacit" (conscious). 17.151

That which is determined to be trees, shrubs, and so forth, devoid of life, is known as *niṣprāṇa* (inanimate) due to its connection with karma; that which is the refuge of the mind and possesses life is remembered as *saprāṇa* (animate).
O Goddess, that consciousness which is the refuge of the individual soul is equal in both [the individual and the universal];
however, the modification of all these principles here arises from the differentiation of the guṇas.
That is indeed accepted as its very nature and is not subject to further questioning;
for aggregates are born from aggregations, and they are many, not of a single form. (17.154)
The primary principles have been declared to you by me; they cannot be fully described.
What is the use of speaking much more here regarding other insentient entities?
In the element of wind, which is of great power and a great being, the world is rendered barren;
it is indeed uncuttable, unburnable, unmoistenable, and even undryable.
He is eternal, omnipresent, and immovable; he is both the sustainer and the awakener.
He is the progenitor of the entire universe and the protector of the entire universe.
The destroyer of the universal wheel, the vast and stainless Lord,
[is the master] of the entire earth with its mountains, islands, oceans, and forests.
O you who are honored by the inhabitants of the earth, these innumerable [beings] are seen established in the wind, which is intent upon bearing the weight of all things. (17.159)
O Mother, it is proclaimed that Māruteśvara itself is present there;
indeed, the entire wheel of light (jyotiścakra) is not moved by the wind.
The wind flows constantly both below and above;
it moves perpetually in some places and remains eternally still in others.
When the bone of the foot reaches a state of attenuation, then the space is the vessel of the foot;
when it flows swiftly with sound, then it is struck. (17.162)
Therefore, this indeed is to be worshipped by yogis for the sake of attaining their own self;
this reality has been declared, as have its other manifestations. (17.163)
Relying upon this, O lady of beautiful hips, the wise should strive for their own welfare;
O daughter of the mountain, the entire established doctrine of the scriptures has been thus declared.
And the entire state of reality has been explained; what more do you wish to hear?
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter in the Ānandatantra.
The eighteenth chapter.
The venerable Goddess said:
O God of gods, O Mahādeva, O bestower of joy upon the world!
Except for whatever else I have touched upon in my heart that remains to be asked. (18.1)
From what does the origin of the world arise—the world consisting of the earth, mountains, and oceans, densely packed and continuous with a multitude of various living beings? (18.2)
It was covered on all sides by numerous trees, shrubs,
and the like, with various species and diverse objects.
In some places it consists of stones and clay, such as boulders and the like;
in some places it is a playful cascade, and in others it is a desert expanse.
Thus, from where has this manifold universe arisen?
O Lord, where does it abide, O All-pervading One? Why does it perish, and why does it not perish? (18.5)
(156)169k) What indeed is the causal root from which this world of moving and non-moving beings arises? Through various conflicting views, O wise one, delusion prevails. // 18.6 //
"You alone are supremely capable of cutting through this doubt of mine;
O Śaṅkara, there is no one other than you who can sever this doubt. (18.7)
O Goddess, the eternal flow of this world is proclaimed as Kāmeśvara;
though ancient, it appears again and again in ever-new forms. (18.8)
O beautiful one, that body of a living being is the righteous form of this world;
indeed, it is the very body of a certain person who conceives the pride of being the universe.
Whatever various states exist within the bodies of living beings, those same states, being identical to them, are established within the Creator of the World. (18.10)
Whatever exists in the egg and in the body of men,
including both heaviness and lightness, there is no difference between the egg and the body.

The difference between the body of an elephant and the like, and the body of a mosquito and the like, which exists by way of measurement— that very same difference indeed exists between the cosmic egg (aṇḍa) and the physical mass (piṇḍa).
Just as the nature of the stream's permanence is perceived by all who have attained realization through the body,
so too is that very same permanence found within the scope of the cosmic egg (aṇḍa).
The bodies of Devadatta and others have been ancient by their very nature; they do not assume a new form, even though they have previously resorted to a prior form. (18.14)
If, due to the distinction between prior and subsequent forms, there were differences in a single Devadatta, then those same differences would apply to the subject at hand as well. (18.15)
In this world, no proponent whatsoever accepts any distinction therein;
those who do so, however, are proclaimed to be fools regarding the proof of momentariness. (18.16)

That which is within the range of the perception of the lump [of clay] called Devadatta has its essence in the form of what preceded it; that essence of the form of what preceded it is the embryo. (18.17)
He is one whose devotion is toward that primordial form; he is the herb that satisfies through that primordial form.
That primordial form is the seed; he is the herb that satisfies through the form of that seed. (18.18)
This stream of seeds and sprouts flows upward;
now let another stream also be understood by you from my words. (18/19)
The prior form of Devadatta’s body was his father;
the prior form of that father was his grandfather, and the prior form of that grandfather was his great-grandfather. (18.20)
Therefore, Devadatta’s eternity exists by way of the continuity of the stream;
and there is also eternity by way of the distinction between the forms of the parts of that stream. (18.21)
Furthermore, in the absence of parts, even the whole does not exist;
for it is the collection of parts that is reckoned as the "whole" by virtue of being a whole. (18.22)
It is not perceived as distinct from the aggregate; even when it is mentally constructed as such, it is not seen separately.
If it were ever perceived anywhere [as distinct], there would be a single nature consisting solely of the word.
O Maheśvarī, this is the course of the body and so forth, O Devadattā;
this very same course applies even to the gross wheel of the universe.
By means of Yajñadatta’s body and the vital fluids contained therein, through the efficacy of the infusion [of that seed], and also by means of his wife’s blood; (18.25)
O beloved, having brought about even the *saṃghāta* [stage] in the form of an embryonic mass, Devadatta then produced it in that same manner for the world. (18.26)
The dissolution of the components of this vast cosmic egg is declared to be the destruction of mental constructs (saṅkalpa) brought about by Māruteśvara. (18.27)

O fair-hipped one, here the essential nature and the multitude of the objects to be qualified—such as the earth and so forth—are always real; however, conjunction and disjunction are distinct from them. (18.28)
When, through contact with the wind, there occurs an embracing by the earth and other elements, then the attainment of the form of an egg takes place; this is declared to be creation. (18.29)
This very Vāyu is the Lord; this very one possesses a body.
As the Sovereign, he unites the elements and he disunites them as well. (18.30)
He is the abode of lights, of darknesses, and of others as well;
his movement is independent and at will, and there is nothing whatsoever that exceeds him.
Whatever form pervades the world belongs to Brahmā, the Supreme Lord;
the exceedingly powerful Vāyu assumes that very same form. (18.32)
There is nothing at all surprising here: the world is seen as if it were a body.
This was the state of the primordial egg; that which is within the egg is said to be its interior. (18.33)

in some cases, when the number of heads is such, the arms are double that number.

Among those deities embraced by Śiva, they are three-eyed and have the moon as their crest-jewel; among those deities embraced by Viṣṇu, they have two eyes due to a difference in meditative visualization.

through the distinctions of their meditations, their waists are bent by their breasts, and their faces resemble the moon. (19.111)
Endowed with amorous attire and adorned with various ornaments, they should be depicted as exceedingly serene, with eyes reddened by intoxication. || 19.112 ||
Among these, one should designate meditation alone as the primary state;

O sweet-spoken one, I have already previously explained that the union of the mind and the vital breath also bestows all accomplishments.

Thus, by means of the five categories beginning with the Guru, which are endowed with meditative cultivation (bhāvanā), [the goal is attained]. (19.115)
The form of the deity, established within the body of the devotee, arises;

180) O Goddess, the intermediate form of the deity is said to be easily accessible;

With a slight anger, he was capable of incinerating the universe in an instant;
with a slight favor, he could bestow the rank of Indra even upon the lowly. (19.121)
O Daughter of the Mountain, she bestows the realization of all reality, the singular discipline of the Great Sacrifice, and the intense form of the deity. (19.122)
In the first [form], they worship for ten years; in the middle, for twenty years;

Thus, O Maheśānī, the reality of the deity has been established by the refutation of the prima facie view; internalize this very truth within yourself.
"Having assumed this form, protect your devoted followers.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter in the Ānandatantra.
Now, O Goddess of the Gods, I shall explain the twentyfold form of the Vidyā, the playful one;
by the thorough knowledge of which secret, all Vidyās grant accomplishment.
This description of the essential nature of the Vidyā which is about to be told—those who hold it in their minds are fortunate devotees. (20.2)

it is like a certain object made of jewels that reflects [the light], but is not itself stained. (20.4)
O lotus-faced one, wherever on this earth there is a sentient being, there is the descent of power (śaktipāta) from Pārvatī;
and even where there is an insentient thing, such as a jewel or the like, it is likewise so.
Elsewhere, because of impurity, the descent of power (śaktipāta) does not occur; however, in this case, the prowess of the descent of power must be directed toward the object, which is water.
One [form of the descent of power] is somewhat bitter to the dull-witted mind, while another is like excellent nectar;
without that descent of power (śaktipāta), how could sweetness ever arise therein?
Having encountered a certain degree of light or darkness, that [light] illuminates its own self; the light of fireflies and stars, for instance, removes only a small amount of darkness. (20.8)
Illuminating the entire universe like a lamp for the jewel of all continents,
he possesses the form of Mārtaṇḍabhairava and is exceedingly difficult to endure due to his splendors.
And from the stars, O Caṇḍāṃśu, the sun of fierce radiance arises;
indeed, it is never seen without the cause that is the descent of power (śaktipāta).
The descent of the power of Māruti occurs when [the breath] is differentiated into prāṇa, apāna, and so forth;
one is Nīla, the destroyer of life, while another is the giver of life.
Alone he is capable of uprooting the wheel of the world with its very foundation;
alone, in a mere moment, he is intent upon the creation of the universe.
Without the descent of power (*śaktipāta*), there is no vision whatsoever in the Lord Māruteśvara; likewise, the descent of power occurs only here and there, and not everywhere. (20.13)
There are indeed many such words; we shall explain their nature, just as the enumeration of the parts of the earth and other elements exceeds that of the worldly cycle.
In the same way, the sound does not enter into the category of worldly things, like the ocean compared to the sounds of drums, kettledrums, small drums, and cymbals. (20.15)
Those sounds produced by musical instruments are not mentioned here;
rather, those sounds consisting of phonemes are eternal and all-pervading.
Qualities are not the cause of anything as separate substances;
even though they are all-pervading, they are not perceived because they depend upon manifestation. (20.17)
And its manifestation occurs within the sphere of the activity of the palate, lips, and so forth;
furthermore, O Great Goddess, its eternity is established by the means of valid cognition known as recognition (pratyabhijñā). || 20.18 ||
The very same syllable *ga*, which was pronounced as a learned excellence by Devadatta, is here proclaimed as a limb [of the word] by Yajñadatta. (20.19)
For recognition is indeed a valid means of knowledge, and it is a direct perception;
therefore, all these words are eternal and also omnipresent.
Behold the world of transmigration, which arises from the mere fifty letters of the word "paśya";
for him whose mass of vision has arisen, even the cosmic egg is but an atom.
O Goddess praised by heroes, the manifestation of the world through earth, water, fire, space, and speech becomes increasingly more extensive at each successive stage.
O lotus-eyed one, even today this ocean of sound continues to expand;
one who is proficient in the Brahman of sound attains the Supreme Brahman. (20.23)
The supreme activity of words is fourfold;
it is divided into thousands of ways through the distinctions of action, quality, and substance.

The fair-complexioned person, the horse, the man, the elephant, the bird, the Brahmin, the deer, the tree, the creeper, and the grass— these are the modifications of the genus arising from sound and the other sense objects.
Kapila, kaḍāra, nīla, śoṇa, pāṇḍara,
dhūmra, pīta, and śyāmala— these have arisen from the quality of sound.
Earth, water, fire, air, sound, darkness, the mind, as well as the sense organs, and the pot, cloth, and wall—these are words denoting substances. (20.27)
Having drunk this ocean of sound—so beautiful with its fourfold divisions—to the very brim of my throat, I am now vomiting it out in this manner. (20.28)
One master is equal to a friend, another is equal to a lover, and yet another is equal to a beloved; indeed, this is remembered as the threefold classification of women. (20.29)
O Maheśvarī, the word is equal to the master, and the heap of the Vedas is that;
O lotus-eyed one, the Āgama is also its very essence.
But one who, like a human being obeying a royal command, does not doubt the supreme meaning of the Vedas and Agamas, considering that sin arises from doubt, [should act accordingly]. (20.31)
Deliberating upon causes and reflecting on what is beneficial and what is harmful, he grasps [the truth] free from fear; by that path, he attains success.
Therefore, this word consisting of the Vedas and Agamas is indeed equal to a master; whereas the word consisting of the scriptures of friends is said to be like the speech of a friend. (20.33)

184k) Regarding this very point concerning Manu, it has been stated in the Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and so forth, by the masters of mantras such as Vyāsa and others who were well-versed in the Purāṇas. (20.34)
One should conduct oneself like Rāma and others, but not like Rāvaṇa and others;
one should follow only the son of Dharma, and not those such as Duryodhana.
He who, like a friend, inspires interest through a single mode of discourse and imparts instruction with affection is one who is equal to a friend. (20.36)
Furthermore, poetry, poetic ornaments, drama, and even the entirety of musical performance as devised by Bharata and others, employ words that are as pleasing as those used for a beloved woman.
That collection [of words], being equal to a beloved in its sweetness, is like a beloved woman through its ornaments, as well as through the *guṇas*, *ritis*, and *vṛttis*. (20.38)
And by various types of beds, by different modes of cooking, and by extremely numerous sounds;
likewise, by the functions of denotation (*abhidhā*), indication (*lakṣaṇā*), and metaphorical transfer (*gauṇī*), as well as by the utterances of the speaker.
Through prose and verse, with various poetic paths that gladden the heart—such as the alliteration of the Lāṭa and Cheka styles and other such compositions—he [attains fame]. (20.40)
Like a clever courtesan, she brings about delight and then imparts beneficial instruction; for whatever is esteemed as womanhood, she performs it all. (20.41)
Through these three modes, the Śabdabrahman proceeds;
yet, within the ocean of Śabdabrahman, the descent of power (śaktipāta) occurs everywhere.
O Guḍākeśa, the nature of mantra resides in certain collections of words distinguished by their sequential order, just as the state of being a jewel exists within a piece of earth.

In these [qualities], there is sweetness as it were, and in those [others], majesty; and having attained them in due order, they are fixed in their intellect according to the path of the Vedas and Agamas.
Although elsewhere it is the words themselves that possess eternity, O Great Goddess, the eternity of their sequence is not likewise [established] here. (20.45)
The eternality of words resides in their sequential order within the collection of mantras;
in the treasury of the universe, the powers of the mantras are known to be their sequential arrangement. (20.46)
Therefore, O Lotus-eyed One, the mantras abide by their inherent nature as the descent of power (śaktipāta), touching upon their fixed sequence. 20.47.
O Ambikā, these mantras of concealment exist here and nowhere else;
however, their manifestation occurs through the instruction of a preeminent teacher.
O Pārvatī, even in the combination of trust, devotion, and worship, you alone are fully manifest;
thus, you are the one in whom your own powers are fully manifested.
All [the goddesses], who sever all defects, bestow every spiritual attainment (siddhi).
In the cleansing of the soot-like darkness of the impurity of beginningless ignorance.
O Lord of the fresh lotus grove, even the drops of water from the seven oceans are counted as mere heaps of mantras compared to your rays.
Furthermore, millions of multitudes of mantra-kings cannot even be counted;
they are all creators of mantras found within the Vedas. (20.52)
Even greater than those are the Vaiṣṇava mantras of the Pañcarātra;
even greater than those, O playful one, are the Saura mantras, which are full of potency.
Even more than those, the mantras dedicated to Gaṇapati bestow success;
even more than those, the mantras of Durgā are intent upon the destruction of miserable states of existence.
Beyond those are the mantras of Śaṅkara, and beyond those, again, the mantras of Śrī;
even beyond those, there would be the most excellent mantras designated as "The All-in-All" (Sarvasva).
Even more powerful than those are the mantras that increase great prosperity;
even more so are the mantras arising from the Eastern Tradition (Pūrvāmnāya), which possess the greatest potency.
Even greater than those are the mantras of the Dakṣiṇāmnāya, which bear the yoke of Śakti;
and even greater than those is the series of mantras of the Paścimāmnāya.
Even more than that, O Maheśvarī, the mantras of the Uttara-āmnāya bestow immense fortune; among them, the Vidyās are like the waters situated within one's own well.
The mantras within the scope of the Śrīcakra are powerful and increase spiritual accomplishments;
among them, the mantras of the fierce Vārtālī are especially bestowers of success. (20.59)
Within those [mantras] also are the Śyāmalā-mantras, which bestow the abundance of intense bliss;
even beyond those are the Lalitā-devis, arising from ten divisions.
The great mantras, which consist of the essential compendium of the wheel of the world, are contained within those two; indeed, this very one is proclaimed as the Great Knowledge (Mahāvidyā).
Just as other kings serve an emperor seated upon the lion-throne for the sake of their own protection and to obtain power themselves, [so do they serve the Lord]. (20.62)
Likewise, all branches of knowledge— the great waves of the Vedas and Āgamas— serve this beloved Vidyā, the Great Goddess who dwells upon the lion-throne.
O Maheśvarī, all the treatises, the entire ocean of traditional scriptures, all the Vedas, and all the Purāṇas [are likewise contained therein].
They praise this very Great Vidyā at every step and distinguish it by its secrecy; yet those of dull intellect do not recognize it. (20.65)
Otherwise, this path of words and its manifestation in the world would be different; those deluded by darkness do not know Lalitā, the Mother of the Vedas. 20/66
She is Sāvitrī for the twice-born, Gāyatrī for those who discourse on Brahman,
Sarasvatī for the lords of poets, and Bhairavī for the yogis.
She is remembered as Śāntā among those called Pāśupatas, as this Śrī among the Jains, as Padmāvatī among the Buddhists, and as Tārā in her flickering moment. (20.68)
This power belongs to the Śāktas; for the Cārvākas, however, it is ontological.
O Great Queen, it belongs to the Sauras and to those who serve the Creator (Brahmā) through faith.
This earth is the domain of those who wield arms and are intent on victory;
what else can it be, but remembered as the plundering deity of thieves? (20.70)
For the heroes of the Ānandāmnāya, Tripurasundarī is manifest;
she who resembles the rising sun has eyes like the stalks of a lotus.
Triangular and adorned with the crescent moon, she is indeed this Supreme Goddess;
O beautiful one, those things which have been declared in the chapter on the Nandī sacrifice— 72. O beautiful one, those things which have been declared in the chapter on the Nandī sacrifice—
The island of Sudhāratnākara, the principal among the [eight] islands, and Mukhyāṇikalabhāṣiṇī—
all these, O Goddess of gods, are known as the city of Śrīcakra.
There, the Lord of Desire is the sovereign god, a treasure-trove of good fortune;
there, Lalitā is the sovereign queen, the dark-hued Mother Pradānā. (20.74)
The goddess Kroḍamukhī, who restrains the wicked and protects the virtuous, guards the city and is intoxicated by the wine of the blood of all her enemies.
The form of royal bliss is the Śrīcakra, the royal capital;
because it protects the sweet meditation, it is the young princess of the king.
The vassal kings shall have faces like those of Kāmeśvarī and the others;
these Śrī-devīs, beginning with Kāmeśvarī, are the most excellent friends of the king. (20.77)
The gods are the primary servants, and there are four goddesses of weaponry;
the goddesses of speech are Vaśinī and the others, while the poets offer charming flatteries.
The great goddesses, beginning with Sarvajñā, are the scholars residing in the royal capital;
the mantras, beginning with Sarvasiddhi, are the ministers skilled in deliberation. (20.79)
The fierce female soldiers of the Command (Ājñā), led by Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī, are the mistresses of the house of the wealth of beauty bestowed upon those who have partaken [of the sacrament]. (20.80)
Through protection, the treasury-guardians are Rahasya, Kusuma, and so forth;
the primary attractors of desire are the nine digits of the cool-rayed moon. (20.81)
O Beloved, the nine principal mudrās—beginning with Mahādevī, who dispels the exhaustion arising from sexual union, and ending with Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī—are the maidservants. 20.82.
O Great Goddess, the powers beginning with *aṇimā* serve as handmaidens for the performance of rites such as summoning and dismissal, acting as a magical illusion for one’s diversion.
The Siddha women, performing various kinds of play, constantly attended upon Brahmā and the other gods in their great enjoyments within the cities. (20.84)
O Mother, those who serve Brahmā and the others according to their respective capacities are elevated as the floors of the celestial palace within the fourteen worlds. (20.85)
This Maheśvarī is the presiding deity of all the worlds;
thus has this Vidyā, the Maheśvarī of the Lion-Throne, been revealed.
Because the path to imperial sovereignty is found within her mantras,
she is therefore renowned throughout the three worlds by the name "Siṃhāsana" (The Lion Throne).
Having established its presence within the heart of this Great Goddess as well,
this Ānandavallī-vidyā contains the essence of all bliss.
This Vidyā is their very nature; there is no difference between them whatsoever.
Ānandadevī is Lalitā, and Lalitā is Ānandabhairavī.
The supreme reality is indeed one; this display of differentiation is false.
Therefore, O Ānanda, this [knowledge] should be cultivated, for it is the sole foundation of the Great Sacrifice (mahāyāga).
Its form consists of all principles (tatvas), and its nature is composed of all bliss.
Awakened by all the scriptures, she bestows the universal self upon the heroes.
She bestows success upon all practitioners by her mere remembrance;
she is sweet when meditated upon and grants accomplishment when spoken of.
When remembered, she alone destroys sin; when practiced, she alone is the nature of dharma.
There exists nothing in the three worlds comparable to her.
This alone is true wisdom, this alone is true cleverness: that a person should, even once, contemplate the Great Knowledge of Bliss. (20.94)
Free from all doubt and devoid of deluded vision, he possesses every auspicious quality; endowed with perfection, he prospers at once.
The King of Sacrifices must be performed for that which consists of bliss, which is radiant,
the supreme abode, and whose nature is consciousness, since the Liṅga is supported by it.
Therefore, O Maheśānī, the Liṅga is always worshipped by yogis;
as are the immortals, the gods, the yakṣas, the rākṣasas, the gandharvas, and the kinnaras. (20.97)
The Mahārājikas, Sādhyas, Rudras, Vasus, Anilas, Niliṃpakas, Pramathas, and all the gods, O Maheśvarī. (20.98)
Various kinds of serpents, beasts, and birds, as well as lions, pythons, goats, tigers, śarabhas, and deer [were there]. (20.99)
Arising from eighty-four hundred thousand different types of birth,
all beings of diverse species consist essentially of pure consciousness vibrating as vital breath.
Since it is true, O Great Goddess, that they worship my liṅga,
therefore, O Pārvatī, from my hands, my feet, my head, and likewise my chest—
From the seat, from the region of the throat, and likewise from the center as it ascends—this is the supreme, most excellent Liṅga; this very one of mine is worshipped.
O Goddess of Gods, even now, among all the great-souled ones who have studied and perceive it, my liṅga is indeed worshipped by them all. (20.103)
Having fashioned a Malliṅga image through self-manifestation (*svayaṃbhū*), mental construction (*kalpana*), and other means,
as well as a *svayaṃbhu-bāṇaliṅga* and likewise a crystal (*sphaṭika*) liṅga.
O Īśānī, there are lingas made of jewels, lingas made of sand, lingas made of gold, lingas made of earth, and likewise lingas made of silver.
In this very manner, O Goddess, a hundred of these lingas and images are worshipped by all who desire every form of prosperity and good fortune.
All this has been told to you; O beloved, whoever recites this, O Mother, whoever hears this, and whoever rejoices in this—[for them all, it shall be so]. (20.107)
He who worships within this very thing the syllables written in a book,
and he who explains the sequence of this subject according to the prescribed rule— [108]
Endowed with all auspiciousness, he shall become the husband of Siddhikāntā;
O Kuleśvarī, this is what you asked regarding the purpose of worshipping my liṅga.
The Samaya has been declared as pure; what more do you wish to hear?
Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Nature of Vidyā," within the thirty-two crore [verse] *Ānandatantra*. The *Ānandatantra* is complete.
